passages.original: 4.Partesorationis primus Aristoteles duas tradidit, nomen et verbum. Deinde Donatus octo definivit. Sed omnes ad illa duo principalia revertuntur, hoc est, ad nomen et verbum, quæ significarit personam et actum. Reliquæ appendices sunt, et ex his originem trahunt.
passages.english: Aristotle was the first to set out two parts of speech, the noun and the verb. Then Donatus defined eight. But all of them go back to those two principal ones, that is, to the noun and the verb, which signify the person and the action. The rest are appendages, and draw their origin from these.
passages.notes: "significarit" read as "significant".

passages.original: 1. Pronomen dictum, quia pro e vice nominis ponitur, ne fastidium faciat nomen ipsum, dum iteratur. Nam cum dicimus : Virgilius scripsit Bucolica, addimus pronomcn, ipse scripsi. et Georgica; sic varietas significationis, cl fastidium tollit, et ornatum inducit.
passages.english: The pronoun is so called because it is put in place of (pro) and instead of the noun, so that the noun itself may not cause tedium by being repeated. For when we say, "Virgil wrote the Bucolics," we add the pronoun, "he himself wrote the Georgics too"; thus variety of signification both removes tedium and brings in ornament.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "pro e vice" read as "pro vice", "pronomcn" as "pronomen", "ipse scripsi." as "ipse scripsit", "cl" as "et".

passages.original: 1. Conjunctio dicta, quod sensus sententiasque conjungat. Hæc enim per se nihil valet, sed in copulatione sermonum, quasi quoddam exhibet glutinum. Aut cnim nomina sociat, ut Augustinus et Hieronymus, aut verba, ut scribit ct legit. Una autem vis omnium, sive copulent, sive disjungant.
passages.english: The conjunction is so called because it joins together (conjungat) meanings and sentences. For by itself it has no force, but in the linking of words it provides a kind of glue. For it either joins nouns, as "Augustine and Jerome," or verbs, as "he writes and reads." And all of them have one force, whether they join or separate.

passages.original: 27. Restant quos a epitrita partitione dividimus: Epitritus primus, ut sacerdotes; Epitritus secundus,ut conditores; Epitritus tertius, ut Demosthenes; Epitritus quartus, ut Feacenninus.
passages.english: There remain those which we divide by the epitrite division: the first epitrite, as sacerdotes; the second epitrite, as conditores; the third epitrite, as Demosthenes; the fourth epitrite, as Fescenninus.
passages.notes: "Feacenninus" read as "Fescenninus"; "a epitrita" read as "epitrita".

passages.original: B. Tetrosyllaba autem , et pentasyllaba ratione trisyllaborum retinentur. f Gravis accentus cum uno accentu poni potest in dictione una, cum utrisque nunquam. ut Catùllus. In composita dictione unus accentus est, ut armipotens, omnipotens.
passages.english: Words of four and five syllables are governed by the rule for those of three syllables. A grave accent can be placed with one [other] accent in a single word, never with both, as Catúllus. In a compound word there is one accent, as armipotens, omnipotens.
passages.notes: The letters "B." and "f" appear to be section or footnote marks and are omitted. The accent rule is compressed and its exact sense is uncertain.

passages.original: In g breviculis quoque quibus militum nomina contionebantur 40 propria nota eratapud veteres, qua inspiceretur quanti ex militibus supereasent, quantique in bello cecidissent. k T nota in capite versiculi posita superstitem designabat. Θ Vero ad uniuscujusque defuncti nomen apponebatur. Unde et habet per medium telum. Id est, mortis signum, de qua Persius ait: Et polis est nigrum vitio præeligere theu.
passages.english: Also in the short lists in which the names of soldiers were contained, the ancients had a particular mark by which it could be seen how many of the soldiers survived and how many had fallen in war. The mark T placed at the head of the line indicated a survivor. But Θ was set beside the name of each one who had died. Hence it also has a spear through the middle, that is, the sign of death, about which Persius says: "And are you able to mark vice with the black theta?"
passages.notes: Footnote marks (g, 40, k) omitted; "contionebantur" read as "continebantur", "supereasent" as "superessent". The Persius quotation is garbled ("Et polis est nigrum vitio præeligere theu"), apparently for "et potis es nigrum vitio praefigere theta"; translated accordingly.

passages.original: 15. 1 Maxumus, an maximus, cet si qua similia sunt, qualiter scribi debeant 45 quæsitum est. Varro tradidit Cæsarem per i hujusmodi verba enuntiare, et scribere solitum esse; inde propter auctoritatcm tanti viri consuetudinem factam ul maximus, optimus, pessimus, scribatur.
passages.english: It has been asked how maxumus or maximus, and any similar words, ought to be written. Varro related that Caesar was accustomed to pronounce and write words of this kind with i; and from this, because of the authority of so great a man, the custom arose that maximus, optimus, pessimus are written [so].
passages.notes: The numerals '15. 1' and '45' are section or footnote marks from the printed edition and have been left out. Read 'et' for 'cet', 'auctoritatem' for 'auctoritatcm', and 'ut' for 'ul'.

passages.original: 14. Paromœon est multitudo verborum ei una lit- Icra inchoantium, quale est apud Ennium : O Tite tute Tati tibi tanta tyranne tulisti.
passages.english: Paromoeon is a multitude of words beginning with one and the same letter, such as is found in Ennius: "O Titus Tatius, tyrant, you yourself brought such things upon yourself."
passages.notes: Read 'et una littera' for 'ei una lit- Icra'. The alliteration of the Ennius line cannot be kept in English.

passages.original: Sed hoc bene temperat Virgilius, dum non toto versu utitur bac figura ut Ennius, sed nunc in principio versus tantum, ut est illud : Sævasedens super arma; nunc in medio, ut : Quæque lacus late liquidos, quæque aspera dumis ; Nunc autem in fine, ut : Sola mihii tales casus Cassandra canebat.
passages.english: But Virgil moderates this well, since he does not use this figure through a whole line as Ennius does, but sometimes only at the beginning of a line, as in that [phrase]: "Fierce, sitting upon arms"; sometimes in the middle, as: "Those which [haunt] the broad clear lakes, and those [haunting] the land rough with thickets"; and sometimes at the end, as: "Cassandra alone used to foretell such fortunes to me."
passages.notes: Read 'Saeva sedens', 'hac' for 'bac', and 'mihi' for 'mihii'.

passages.original: Similitudo autem tribus modis fit ; a pari, a majore, a minore. A pari: Ac veluti magno in populo cum sæpe coorta est Seditio. A majore ad minus: Qualiter expressum venti, per nubila fulmen ; a minore ad majus : Si ponit manes arcessere conjugis Orpheus Threicia fretus cithara fidibusque canoris quasi dicat, re parva et brevi, id est, si ille cithara fretUs, ego pietate.
passages.english: Similitude is made in three ways: from the equal, from the greater, from the lesser. From the equal: "And as when often in a great people a riot has arisen." From the greater to the lesser: "As a thunderbolt squeezed out by the winds through the clouds"; from the lesser to the greater: "If Orpheus could summon the shade of his wife, relying on his Thracian lyre and its tuneful strings," as if he were saying: by a small and slight thing, that is, if he [could do it] relying on a lyre, [why not] I [relying] on devotion.
passages.notes: "ponit" read as "potuit". The closing explanation is elliptical and the bracketed supplements are interpretive.

passages.original: I. Prosa est producta oratio, et a lege metri soluta. b Prosum enim antiqui productum dicebant, et rectum. Unde ait Yarro apud Plautum prosis lectis significare rectis ; unde etiam quas non est perflexa numero, sed recta, prosa oratio dicitur, in rectum producendo, Alii prosam aiunt dictam ab eo quod sit profusa, vel ab eo quod spatiosius proruat et excurrat, nullo sibi termino præfinito.
passages.english: Prose is drawn-out speech, freed from the law of metre. For the ancients called what was drawn out and straight prosum. Hence Varro says that in Plautus prosis lectis means 'straight [couches]'; hence also speech which is not bent by rhythm but straight is called prose, from drawing out in a straight line. Others say prose is so called from its being profuse, or from its rushing forth and running on more expansively, with no limit set for it beforehand.
passages.notes: "b" footnote mark omitted; "Yarro" read as "Varro", "quas non est perflexa" as "quae non est perflexa".

passages.original: A numero vero hexametrum, pentametrum, trimetrum. Nam senarios versus nos ex numero pedum vocamus; nos Græci g qnia geminos feriunt, trimetros dicunt. Hexametros autem Latinos primum fecisse Ennius traditur, h eosque sangos vocat.
passages.english: From number, however, [metres are called] hexameter, pentameter, trimeter. For we name senarii from the number of feet; the Greeks, because they strike [the feet] in pairs, call them trimeters. Ennius is said to have been the first to compose Latin hexameters, and he calls them 'longs'.
passages.notes: Stray letters 'g' and 'h' are footnote marks. 'nos Graeci' is evidently corrupt for 'Graeci' and is translated so. 'sangos' is corrupt; it presumably stands for 'longos' ('longs'), and is translated so.

passages.original: 24. i Clausulasautem Lyrici appellant, quasi præcisos versus integris subjectos, ut est apud Horatium : Beatus ille qui procul negotiis, deinde sequitur præcisus : Ut prisca gens mortalium. Sic et deinceps alterni, quibus aliqua pars deest, et ipsi præcedentibus similes, sed minores.
passages.english: Lyric poets call clausulae, as it were, cut-short lines placed after full ones, as in Horace: "Happy is he who, far from business," then follows the shortened one: "like the ancient race of mortals." So also thereafter alternate [lines], from which some part is lacking, themselves like the preceding ones, but shorter.
passages.notes: Footnote mark "i" omitted.

passages.original: 3. Fabulas poetae quasdam delectandi causa finxerunt, quasdam ad naturam rerum, nonnullas ad mores hominum interpretati sunt. Delectandi causa fictæ, ut eæ quas vulgo dicunt, vel quales Plautus et Terentius composuerunt.
passages.english: Poets invented some fables for the sake of giving pleasure, and interpreted some with reference to the nature of things, some with reference to human morals. Those invented for the sake of pleasure are such as those that people commonly tell, or such as Plautus and Terence composed.

passages.original: 72 6. Ad mores, ut apud Horatium mus loquitur muri, mustella vulperculæ, ut per narrationem fictam ad id quod agitur verax significatio referatur. Unde et Æsopi tales fabulae sunt ad morum finem relatæ ; vel sicut in libro Judicum ligna sibi regem requirunt, et loquuntur ad oleam, et ad ficum , et ad vitem, et ad rubum : quod lotum utique ad mores fingitur , ut ad rcm quae intenditur, ficta quidem narratione, sed veraci significatione, veniatur.
passages.english: 6. [Some fables are composed] with a view to morals, as in Horace a mouse speaks to a mouse, a weasel to a little fox, so that through a fictitious narrative a true meaning may be applied to the matter in hand. Hence also the fables of Aesop are of this kind, directed to a moral end; or as in the book of Judges the trees seek a king for themselves, and speak to the olive, and to the fig, and to the vine, and to the bramble: the whole of this is certainly invented with a view to morals, so that one may arrive at the thing intended by a narrative that is indeed fictitious, but with a true meaning.
passages.notes: The leading '72' appears to be a page or column number. 'lotum' read as 'totum' and 'rcm' as 'rem' (scanning errors). 'vulperculae' (little fox) presumably for 'vulpeculae'.

passages.original: i. Tripartita controversia, juxta Ciceronem, aut simplex est, aut conjuncta. Et si conjuncta erit, considerandum est utrum sit ex pluribus quaestionibus juncta, an ex aliqua comparatione. Controversia simplex est quæ absolutam continet unam quæstionem, hoc modo : Corinthiis bellum indicamus, an non ?
passages.english: 1. A controversy, according to Cicero, is threefold: it is either simple or conjoined. And if it is conjoined, one must consider whether it is joined from several questions or from some comparison. A simple controversy is one that contains a single self-contained question, in this way: Shall we declare war on the Corinthians, or not?

passages.original: 10. Convincibilc est quod evidenti ratione convincit, sicut fecit Cicero pro Milone : Ejus igitur mortis sedetis ultores, cujus vitam, si putaretis per vos restitui posse, nolletis.
passages.english: 10. The "convincing" [argument] is one that proves by evident reasoning, as Cicero did in the speech for Milo: "You sit, then, as avengers of the death of a man whose life, if you thought it could be restored by you, you would not want [restored]."
passages.notes: "Convincibilc" read as "Convincibile".

passages.original: ii. Ostentabile est quod certa rei demonstratione constringit, sicut Cicero in Catilinam : Hic tamen vivit, vivit, imo etiam in senatum venit. Sententiale est quod sententia generalis addicit, ut apud Terentium : Obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit.
passages.english: 11. The demonstrative [kind] is that which binds by a sure demonstration of the matter, as Cicero [says] against Catiline: 'Yet this man lives; he lives, indeed he even comes into the senate.' The sententious [kind] is that which a general maxim adds, as in Terence: 'Compliance breeds friends, truth hatred.'
passages.notes: The section number 'ii' is probably a misreading of '11'.

passages.original: 12. Exemplabile est quod alicujus exempli compa- ratione eventum similem comminatur, sicut d Cicero in Philippic.: Te miror, Antoni, quarum exempla imitaris, eorum exitus non pertimescere.
passages.english: 12. The exemplary [kind] is that which, by comparison with some example, threatens a similar outcome, as Cicero [says] in the Philippics: 'I am amazed, Antony, that you do not dread the end of those whose examples you imitate.'
passages.notes: Stray footnote mark 'd' omitted.

passages.original: 13. Collectivum est cum in unum quæ e argumentata sunt colliguntur, sicut ait Cicero pro Milone : Quem igitur cum gratia noluit, hunc voluit cum aliquorum querela. Quem jure, quem loco, quem tempore non est ausus, hunc injuria, alieno tempore, cum periculo capitis non dubitavit occidere!
passages.english: 13. The collective [kind] is when the things that have been argued are gathered into one, as Cicero says in the speech for Milo: 'So the man whom he was unwilling [to kill] with people's goodwill, him he was willing [to kill] with some people's complaint. The man whom he did not dare [to kill] lawfully, in a fitting place, at a fitting time, him he did not hesitate to kill unlawfully, at an unfavourable time, at the risk of his own life!'
passages.notes: Stray footnote mark 'e' omitted.

passages.original: 21. Aliae a derogativae, ut, nequaquam. Aliae, quae cum exclamatione proferuntur, ut : b Quis furor, o cives, pacem convertit in arma ? Et Cicero : 0 dii immortales, ubinam gentium sumus ?
passages.english: 21. Others are negative, such as 'by no means'. Others are uttered with an exclamation, such as: 'What madness, citizens, has turned peace into arms?' And Cicero: 'O immortal gods, where in the world are we?'
passages.notes: Stray footnote marks 'a' and 'b' omitted; '0' read as 'O'. The subject (probably kinds of sentences or adverbs) is not stated in the passage.

passages.original: 31. Paradoxon est, cum dicimus inopinatum aliquid accidisse, ut pro Flacco Cicero : Cujus laudis prædicator esse debuerit, ejus periculi deprecatorem use factum.
passages.english: 31. Paradoxon is when we say that something unexpected has happened, as Cicero [says] in the speech for Flaccus: 'He of whose praise he ought to have been the herald, of his peril he has become the intercessor.'
passages.notes: 'use' read as 'esse' (scanning error). The quotation is obscure out of context.

passages.original: 33. Parrhesia est oratio libertalis et fiduciæ plena: k Occidi, occidi non Spurium Melium, etc. Qua figura caute utendum est, ut Cicero, praemisit enim rationem.
passages.english: 33. Parrhesia is speech full of freedom and confidence: 'I have killed, I have killed, not Spurius Maelius,' etc. This figure must be used cautiously, as Cicero [did], for he set out his reasoning first.
passages.notes: Stray footnote mark 'k' omitted; 'libertalis' read as 'libertatis'.

passages.original: 1 Metathesis est quae mittit animos judicum in res præteritas, aut futuras, hoc modo : Revocate mentes ad spectaculum expugnatæ miseræ civitatis, et videre vos credite incendia, cædes, rapinas, direptiones, liberorum corporum injurias, captivitates matronarum, trucidatione, senum. In futurum autem anticipatio eorum quæ dicturus est adversarius, ut Tullius pro Milone, cum mittit animos judicum in eum reipublicae statum qui futurus esset, si, occiso Milone, Clodius viveret.
passages.english: 35. Metathesis is that which sends the minds of the judges to things past or future, in this way: 'Recall your minds to the spectacle of the storming of the wretched city, and believe that you see fires, slaughters, plunderings, lootings, outrages on the bodies of the freeborn, captivities of matrons, the butchery of old men.' But [with regard] to the future, [it is] the anticipation of what the opponent is going to say, as Tullius [does] in the speech for Milo, when he sends the minds of the judges to that state of the republic which would come about if, Milo having been killed, Clodius were alive.
passages.notes: Section number '35' taken from context; leading '1' appears to be a stray mark. 'trucidatione' read as 'trucidationes'.

passages.original: 41. b Epitrochassus, cum plures sensus breviter expeditos in unum locum coacervat, et cum quadam festinatione decurrit, ut Cicero : Rempublicam, Qui- nites, vitamque omnium vestram, bona, fortunas, conjuges, liberosque vestros, etc.
passages.english: 41. Epitrochasmus [is] when one heaps together in one place several ideas briefly dispatched and runs through them with a certain haste, as Cicero [says]: 'The republic, citizens, and the life of all of you, your goods, fortunes, wives and children,' etc.
passages.notes: 'Epitrochassus' read as 'Epitrochasmus'; stray footnote mark 'b' omitted; 'Qui- nites' read as 'Quirites'.

passages.original: 5. 107 Nomen est vox significativa secundum placitum, sine tempore, cujus nulla pars significativa separata, ut Socrates. Verbum est quod significat tempus, cujus pars nihil extra significat, sed semper eorum quæ de altero dicuntur nota est, ut cogitat, disputat. Oralio est vox significativa, cujus partium aliquid separatum significativum est, ut Socrates disputat.
passages.english: A noun is a sound that signifies by convention, without time, no part of which signifies when separated, as 'Socrates'. A verb is what signifies time, no part of which signifies anything on its own; and it is always a sign of the things said of something else, as 'thinks', 'disputes'. A statement is a sound that signifies, some part of which signifies when separated, as 'Socrates disputes'.
passages.notes: '5. 107' is a section and footnote mark. Read 'Oratio' for 'Oralio'.

passages.original: 6. Affirmatio est enuntiatio alicujus de aliquo, ut Socrates est; negalio est alicujus ab aliquo, ut Socrates non est. Contradictio est affirmationis et negationis oppositio, ut Socrates disputat, Socrates non disputat. 7. e Hæc omnia in libro perihermeniarum minutissime divisa et subdivisa tractantur, quarum rerum definitiones hic breviter sufficiat intimasse, quando in ipso competens explanatio reperitur.
passages.english: An affirmation is the stating of something about something, as 'Socrates is'; a negation is [the stating] of something away from something, as 'Socrates is not'. A contradiction is the opposition of an affirmation and a negation, as 'Socrates disputes, Socrates does not dispute'. All these things are treated, divided and subdivided in the finest detail, in the book Perihermeneias; let it suffice here to have briefly set out their definitions, since a fitting explanation is found in that book itself.
passages.notes: Read 'negatio' for 'negalio'. The stray 'e' is a footnote mark. 'Perihermeneias' is Aristotle's On Interpretation.

passages.original: 8. Septima species definitionis est quam Græci ϰατὰ μεταϕορὰν, Latini per translationem dicunt, ut Cicero in Top. : Littus est, d qua fluctus eludit. Haec varie tractari potest: modo enim ut moneat, modo ut designet, modo ut laudet ac vituperet. Ut moneat: Nobilitas est virtus majorum apud posteros sarcina.
passages.english: 8. The seventh kind of definition is the one the Greeks call *kata metaphoran* and the Latins "by transference," as Cicero in the Topics: "The shore is where the wave plays." This can be handled in various ways: sometimes so as to admonish, sometimes so as to indicate, sometimes so as to praise or to blame. So as to admonish: "Nobility is the virtue of ancestors, a burden upon their descendants."
passages.notes: The stray "d" before "qua" is a footnote mark and has been omitted. "Eludit" ("plays") is the text as given; Cicero's Topics has "eludat."

passages.original: 13. Duodecima species definitionis est quam Graeci ϰατ' ἐπαίνον vocant, id est per laudem, Ut Tullius prd Cluentio : Lex est mens, et consilium, et animus, et sententia civitatis; et aliter : Pax est tranquilla libertas. Fit el per vituperationem, quam Græci ϕόγον vocant, ut : Servitus est postremum omnium malorum, non modo bello sed morte quoque repellenda.
passages.english: 13. The twelfth kind of definition is the one the Greeks call *kat' epainon*, that is, "by praise," as Tully in the speech for Cluentius: "Law is the mind and counsel and spirit and judgement of the state"; and elsewhere: "Peace is tranquil liberty." It is also made by blame, which the Greeks call *psogos*, as: "Slavery is the last of all evils, to be warded off not only by war but even by death."
passages.notes: "prd" has been read as "pro" and "el" as "et" (scanning errors). The printed "ϕόγον" stands for ψόγον (psogos, "blame").

passages.original: i. Argumentum a toto, cum definitio adhibetur ad id quod quæritur, sicut ait Cicero : a Gloria est laus recte factorum, magnorumque in rempublicam fama meritorum.
passages.english: i. The argument from the whole: when a definition is applied to the thing under inquiry, as Cicero says: "Glory is the praise of things rightly done, and the fame of great services to the state."
passages.notes: The stray "a" is a footnote mark and has been omitted. The section number "i." is as printed; it may be a misread "1."

passages.original: 4. A nota est argumentum, cum eivi nominis argumentum aliquod elicitur, ut Cicero Consulem, inquit, quærebam, quem c inito majali invenire non poteram.
passages.english: 4. The argument is from the sign [of a name] when some argument is drawn out of a name, as Cicero: "I was looking for a consul," he says, "whom I could not find, once the Kalends of May had begun."
passages.notes: "eivi" has been read as "ex vi" ("from the force [of a name]"). "majali" is uncertain; it is perhaps a corruption, and the sense of the quotation is unclear. The stray "c" is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: 5. Affecta argumenta sunt quae quodammodo ex rebus aliis tracta noscuntur. Sunt autem numero quatuordecim, id est: primum a conjugatis argumentum est, cum declinatur a nomine, et fit verbum, ut Cicero Verrem dicit everrisse provinciam; vel nomen a verbo, cum latrocinari dicitur latro. Nomen est a nomine; Terentius : d Inceptio est amentium, haud amantium , dummodo distet unius appellationis postremitas in aliam vocis declinationem formata.
passages.english: 5. Related arguments are those recognised as drawn in some way from other things. They are fourteen in number. The first is the argument from conjugates, when [a word] is derived from a noun and a verb is made, as Cicero says that Verres "swept out" (everrisse) the province; or a noun from a verb, as when one who plunders (latrocinari) is called a robber (latro). [Or] a noun from a noun; Terence: "It is a scheme of the mad (amentium), not of lovers (amantium)," provided that the ending of the one name differs, formed into another declension of the word.
passages.notes: The stray "d" is a footnote mark and has been omitted. The Terence line normally reads "inceptio est amentium, haud amantium." The final clause is obscure.

passages.original: 6. Secundum argumentum a genere est, cum de eodem genere sententia dicitur, ut Virgilius : Varium et mutabile semper femina.
passages.english: 6. The second argument is from genus, when a statement is made about the same genus, as Virgil: "A fickle and ever-changing thing is woman."

passages.original: 115 8. A differentia argumentum est quando per differentiam aliqua separantur, ut Virgilius : Non Diomedis equos, nec currum cernis Achillis. A contrariis argumentum ducitur, quando res discrepantes sibimet opponuntur, ut Virgilius : Mortaline manu factæ immortale carinæ Faa habeant, certusque incerta pericula lustret Æneas ?
passages.english: 8. The argument from difference is when some things are separated by their difference, as Virgil: "You do not see the horses of Diomedes, nor the chariot of Achilles." The argument from contraries is drawn when discordant things are set against one another, as Virgil: "Are ships made by mortal hand to have immortal rights, and is Aeneas, certain, to pass through uncertain perils?"
passages.notes: The leading "115" is a page number. "Faa" has been read as "fas" ("rights").

passages.original: 9. A consequentibus argumentum ducitnr, quando positam rem aliquid in evitabiliter consequitur, aC Virgilius : Non ea vis animo, nec tanta superbia victis. Ab antecedentibus argumentum est quando aliqua ex iis quæ prius gesta sunt comprobantur, ut Cicero pro Milone : Cum non dubitaverit aperire quid cogitaverit, vos potestis dubitare quid fecerit ?
passages.english: 9. The argument from consequents is drawn when something inevitably follows upon a thing posited, as Virgil: "Such force is not in [our] minds, nor such arrogance in the vanquished." The argument from antecedents is when certain things are proved from those that were done earlier, as Cicero in the speech for Milo: "Since he did not hesitate to disclose what he had planned, can you hesitate [about] what he did?"
passages.notes: "ducitnr" has been read as "ducitur", "in evitabiliter" as "inevitabiliter" and "aC" as "ut".

passages.original: 10. A repugnantibus argumentum est quando illud quod objicitur aliqua contrarietate destruitur, ut Cicero: e Is igitur non modo de tali periculo liberatus, sed honore amplissimo ditatus domi te interficere voluisset ?
passages.english: 10. The argument from incompatibles is when what is alleged is destroyed by some contradiction, as Cicero: "Would he, then, not only freed from such danger but enriched with the highest honour, have wanted to kill you in his own house?"
passages.notes: The stray "e" is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: 11. A conjunctis argumentum est cum probabiliter ostenditur quid sit exre quaqne venturum, ut Virgilius: ..... Nos si pellant, nihil abfore credunt Quin omnem Hesperiam penitus sua sub juga mittant.
passages.english: 11. The argument from conjoined things is when it is shown as probable what will come of each matter, as Virgil: "... If they drive us out, they believe nothing will prevent them from sending all Hesperia utterly under their yoke."
passages.notes: "exre quaqne" has been read as "ex re quaque". The dots are as printed in the edition.

passages.original: A cauti sargumentum est, quando consuetudine communi res quaeque tractatur, ut Tereut. : Ego nonnihil veritus sum dudum abs te, Dave, Ne faceres quod vulgus servorum solet, dolis, Ut me deluderes. Ab effectis argumentum est cum ex iis quæ facta sunl aliquid approbatur, ut Virgilius : Degeneres animos timor arguit.
passages.english: An argument from the customary is when each thing is treated according to common custom, as in Terence: "I have been somewhat afraid for a while, Davus, that you might do what the common run of slaves usually do, and deceive me with tricks." An argument from effects is when something is proved from things that have been done, as Virgil [says]: "Fear proves souls base-born."
passages.notes: "A cauti" is evidently a scanning error, probably for "a consueto" (from the customary), which fits the definition; translated accordingly. "Tereut." = Terence; "sunl" = "sunt".

passages.original: 1. Conlrariorum genera quatuor sunt, quæ Aristoteles ἀντιϰείμενα, id est opposita vocat, propterea quod sibi velut ex adverso videntur obsistere, ut contraria. Nec tamen omnia quæ sibi opponuntur contraria sunt, sed omnia contraria opposita sunt. Primum genus est contrariorum, a quod, juxta Ciceronem adversum vocatur, pro eo 117 quod tantum contrarie sibi opponuntur, ut non eorum sint quibus opponuntur, ut sapientia, stultitia.
passages.english: 1. There are four kinds of contraries, which Aristotle calls *antikeimena*, that is, "opposites", because they seem to stand against one another as if from opposite sides, like contraries. Yet not all things that are opposed to one another are contraries, but all contraries are opposites. The first kind of contraries is the one which, following Cicero, is called "adverse", because they are opposed to one another only contrarily, in such a way that they do not belong to the things to which they are opposed, as wisdom and folly.
passages.notes: The stray letter "a" and the number "117" are footnote or page marks and have been omitted. The clause "ut non eorum sint quibus opponuntur" is obscure; the translation is literal.

passages.original: 6. Tertium genus oppositorum est habitus, vel orbatio. Quod genus Cicero privationem vocat, quia ostendit aliquid quempiam habuisse unde privatus est. Cujus species sunt tres, quarum prima est in re, secunda in loco, tertia in temporecongruo. In re, ut cæ- cilas, et visio.In loco, ut : « Cæcitatis et visionis inoculis locus est.» In tempore congruo, ut: < Infantem non dicere sine dentibus eum 118 cui dentes ætas adhuc parva negavit;
passages.english: 6. The third kind of opposites is possession and deprivation. Cicero calls this kind "privation", because it shows that someone had something of which he has been deprived. It has three species: the first is in the thing, the second in the place, the third in the appropriate time. In the thing, as blindness and sight. In the place, as: "The place of blindness and of sight is in the eyes." In the appropriate time, as: "Not to call an infant toothless when his still tender age has denied him teeth;
passages.notes: The number "118" is a page mark and has been omitted. The final sentence breaks off; the following context continues: "for he has not been deprived of teeth that he has not yet had."

passages.original: 7. « Quartum vero genus ex affifmatione et negatione opponitur, ut: Socrates disputat, Socrates non disputat. Hæc a superioribus ideo differunt, quod illa singulatim dici possunt, haec nisi connexe dici non possunt. Quod genus quartum apud dialecticos inultum habet conflictum, et appellatur ab eis valde oppositum, siquidem et tertium non recipit.
passages.english: The fourth kind [of opposites] is opposed by affirmation and negation, as: 'Socrates disputes, Socrates does not dispute'. These differ from the preceding ones in that those can be said separately, while these cannot be said except in connection. This fourth kind involves much conflict among the dialecticians, and is called by them 'strongly opposed', since it does not admit a third [possibility] either.
passages.notes: Read 'affirmatione' and 'multum' for the misprints.

passages.original: i. Moyses dicit repertorem musicae artis fuisse Jubal, qui fuit de stirpe Cain ante diluvium. d Græci vero Pythagoram dicunt hujus arlis invenisse primordia, ex malleorum sonitu, et cordarum extensione percussa. Alii eLinum Thebæum, et f Zethum, et Amphiona in arte musica prin os claruisse ferunt.
passages.english: 1. Moses says that the inventor of the art of music was Jubal, who was of the line of Cain, before the Flood. The Greeks, however, say that Pythagoras discovered the beginnings of this art from the sound of hammers and from the striking of stretched strings. Others report that Linus of Thebes, Zethus and Amphion were the first to become famous in the art of music.
passages.notes: Stray letters "d", "e" and "f" are footnote marks. "prin os" is read as "primos" (first).

passages.original: Chordarum etiam numerus multiplicatus est, et commutatum geuus. Veteres autem citharam fidiculam vel fidem nominaverunt, quia tam concinunt inter se chordae ejus, quam bene conveniunt inter quos fides sit. Antiqua autem cithara septem chordis erat; unde Virgilius : Septem discrimina vocum.
passages.english: The number of strings was also multiplied, and the kind [of instrument] was changed. The ancients called the cithara *fidicula* or *fides*, because its strings sound together with one another as well as those people agree among whom there is good faith (*fides*). The ancient cithara had seven strings; hence Virgil: "The seven distinct notes."
passages.notes: The wordplay is on fides, which means both "string" and "good faith".

passages.original: 12. Sistrum ab inventrice vocatum. Isis enim Ægy- ptiorom regina id genus invenisse probatur. Juvenalis : Isis, et irato feriat mea limina sistro. Inde et hoc mulieres percutiunt, quia inventrix hujus generis mulier. n Unde, et apud Amazonas sistro ad bellum feminarum exercitus vocabatur.
passages.english: 12. The sistrum is named after its inventor. For Isis, queen of the Egyptians, is shown to have invented this kind [of instrument]. Juvenal: "And may Isis strike my doorway with her angry sistrum." For this reason women also play it, because the inventor of this kind [of instrument] was a woman. Hence also among the Amazons the army of women was called to war by the sistrum.
passages.notes: The stray "n" is a footnote mark. The etymology from Isis's name is not clear from the text as given.

passages.original: i. Facies cœli, vel caput, orientalis regio ; mul- lima septentrionalis. De qua Lucanus : Sic mundi pars ima facet, qnam zona nivalis, Perpetuæque premunt hiemes.
passages.english: 1. The face, or head, of the sky is the eastern region; the lowest [part] is the northern. Of which Lucan [says]: "So the lowest part of the world lies, which the snowy zone and everlasting winters press down."
passages.notes: "mullima" is read as "ultima" (the lowest or furthest part); "facet" as "iacet"; "qnam" as "quam".

passages.original: e Hyadcs dictae ἀπὸ τοῡ υ̃ειν, id est, a succo, et pluviis. Nam pluvia Graece ὑετὸς dicitur. Ortu quippe suo efficiunt pluvias, unde et eas Latini succulas appellaverunt, quia quando nascuntur, pluviarum signa monstrantur, de quibus Virgilius : Arcturum pluviasque Hyadas. Sunl autem septem in fronte Tauri, et oriuntur tempore vernali.
passages.english: The Hyades are named from *hyein*, that is, from moisture and rains. For rain in Greek is called *hyetos*. For by their rising they bring about rains; hence the Latins also called them *Suculae*, because when they arise, signs of rain are shown. Of them Virgil [says]: "Arcturus and the rainy Hyades." They are seven, on the forehead of Taurus, and they rise in springtime.
passages.notes: The stray "e" is a footnote mark. The text has "succulas", linked to "succus" (moisture); the usual spelling is Suculae.

passages.original: i llesperus stella occidentalis, quam cognominatam perhibent ab Hespero Hispaniæ rege. Estautcm, et ipsa ex quinque stellis planetis, noclem ducens, et solem sequens. Fertur autem quod haec stella oriens Luciferam, occidens vesperum facit, de qua Statius : .... et alterno deperditur unus iu ortu.
passages.english: 1. Hesperus is the western star, which they say was named after Hesperus, a king of Spain. It too is one of the five planets; it leads in the night and follows the sun. It is said that this star, when rising, makes Lucifer [the morning star], and when setting, Vesper [the evening star]. Of it Statius [says]: "... and the one is lost in the alternate rising."
passages.notes: The quotation from Statius is fragmentary and its sense is uncertain.

passages.original: 2. Thymiama lingua Græca vocatur, quod sit odorabile. Nam thymus dicitur Dos, qui odorem refert, de quo Virgilius: .... redolentque thymo fragrantia mella.
passages.english: 2. *Thymiama* [incense] is so called in the Greek language because it is fragrant. For the flower that gives off scent is called *thymus* [thyme]. Of it Virgil [says]: "... and the fragrant honey smells of thyme."
passages.notes: "Dos" is read as "flos" (flower).

passages.original: G. Myrobalanum, quia fit ex glande adorata, do quo Horatius : Et pressa tuis balanus capillis. Oleum est purum, nullique rei admistum. Unguentum vero est omne quod ex communi oleo confectum, aliarum specierum commistione augetur, odoris jucunditatem sumens, et longius redolens.
passages.english: Myrobalanum [is so called] because it is made from a fragrant acorn (glans), of which Horace [says]: "And balanus pressed for your hair." Oil is [something] pure, mixed with nothing. But ointment is everything that is made from common oil and enhanced by mixing in other spices, taking on a pleasant scent and keeping its fragrance longer.
passages.notes: The initial "G." is probably a section or footnote mark and has been omitted. "do quo" read as "de quo" and "adorata" as "odorata" (fragrant).

passages.original: i. Satyra g vero lex est quæ de pluribus rebla simul eloquitur, dicta a copia rerum, et h quasi a saturitate; uude, i et satyram scribere est poemata varia condere, ut Horatii, Juvenalis et Persii.
passages.english: A satura law is one that deals with many matters at once, named from the abundance (copia) of its matters and, as it were, from fullness (saturitas). Hence also to write satire is to compose varied poems, like those of Horace, Juvenal and Persius.
passages.notes: Stray letters (i, g, h, i) are taken as footnote marks. "rebla" read as "rebus", "uude" as "unde".

passages.original: Cessio est propriæ rei concesso , sicut est illud : Cedo jure propinquitatis. Cedere enim dicimus, quasi concedere, id est , quae propria sunt ; nam aliena restituimus, non cedimus. Nam cederc proprie dicitur , qui contra veritatem alteri consentit , ut i Cicero : Cessit, inquit, amplissimi viri auctoritati, vel potius paruit.
passages.english: Cession is the yielding up of one's own property, as in the phrase: "I cede by right of kinship." For we say "to cede" as if "to concede," that is, things that are our own; for we restore what belongs to others, we do not cede it. For he is properly said to cede who agrees with another against the truth, as Cicero [says]: "He yielded," he says, "to the authority of a most distinguished man, or rather obeyed it."
passages.notes: "concesso" read as "concessio"; "cederc" as "cedere"; stray "i" before Cicero omitted.

passages.original: 15. k Raptus proprie est illicitus coitus, a corrum- pendo dictus, unde Virgilius : Rapto potitur, id est, stupro fruitur.
passages.english: Rape (raptus) is properly unlawful intercourse, named from corrupting (corrumpendo); hence Virgil: "He enjoys the seizure," that is, he enjoys the violation.
passages.notes: Stray "k" omitted. The derivation of raptus from corrumpendo is Isidore's own.

passages.original: Accusatorem ejus possessio bonorum sequebatur. Internecivi autem significatio est, quasi hominis quaedam enecatio; nam præpositionem inter ponebant antiqui pro e. Nævius : Mare INTER-bibere. Et Plautus : INTERluere mare, id est, ebihere, et eluere.
passages.english: The possession of his property went to his accuser. The meaning of internecivus is, as it were, a kind of killing-off of a person; for the ancients used the preposition inter in place of e. Naevius: "to inter-drink the sea." And Plautus: "to inter-wash the sea," that is, to drink up and to wash out.
passages.notes: "ebihere" read as "ebibere". The passage explains internecivus via enecatio.

passages.original: 4. e Octo genera poenarum in legibus contineri Tullius scribit : 213 damnum, vincula, verbera, talionem, ignominium, exsilium, servitutem, et mortem; his namque poenis vindicatur omne perpetratum peccatum.
passages.english: 4. Tullius writes that eight kinds of penalty are contained in the laws: fine, chains, flogging, retaliation, disgrace, exile, slavery, and death; for by these penalties every crime committed is punished.
passages.notes: Tullius is Cicero. The stray 'e' and '213' are print marks.

passages.original: fama autem dicta, quia fando, id est, loquendo, pervagatur per traduces linguarum et aurium serpens. Est autem nomen et bonarum rerum, et malarum. Nam fama felicitatis interdum est, « at illud eat: Illustris fama, quod laus est; malarum, ut Virgilius : Fama malo, qua a non aliud velocius ullum.
passages.english: Fame (fama) is so called because it wanders about by speaking (fando), that is, by talking, creeping along the channels of tongues and ears. It is a name for both good things and bad. For there is sometimes a fame of good fortune, as in the phrase "illustrious fame," which is praise; [and fame] of bad things, as Virgil [says]: "Rumour, an evil than which nothing else is swifter."
passages.notes: "« at illud eat" read as "ut illud est"; "malo, qua a non" as "malum, qua non" (Virgil, Aeneid 4.174).

passages.original: k Noctem autem fieri, aut quia longo itinere lassa- tur sol, et cum ad ultimum coeli spatium pervenit elanguescit, ac labefactos efflat suos ignes; aut quia eadem vi sub terras cogitur, qua super terras pertulit lumen, et sic umbra terrae noctem facit. Unde et Virgilius : Ruit Oceano nox, Involvens umbra magna terramque polumque.
passages.english: Night occurs either because the sun grows tired from its long journey and, when it reaches the farthest region of the sky, grows faint and breathes out its weakened fires; or because it is driven under the earth by the same force by which it carried its light above the earth, and so the shadow of the earth makes night. Hence also Virgil: "Night rushes from the Ocean, enveloping in great shadow both earth and sky."
passages.notes: Stray "k" omitted. The opening infinitive "fieri" implies a preceding verb of saying (e.g. "they say").

passages.original: 21. Horum autem trium librorum carmina hexametris et pentametris versibus apud suos composita perhibentur, ut Josephus, Hieronymusque scribunt.
passages.english: The poems of these three books are said to have been composed among their own people in hexameter and pentameter verses, as Josephus and Jerome write.
passages.notes: The three books are not identified in the passage (probably biblical poetic books).

passages.original: i. Marcus o Terentius Varro apud Latinos ipnumerabiles libros scripsit. Apud Graecos quoque Chalcenterus miris attollitur laudibus, quod tantos libros ediderit quantos quisque uosurum alienos scribere propria manu vix possit.
passages.english: Among the Latins, Marcus Terentius Varro wrote innumerable books. Among the Greeks too, Chalcenterus is extolled with wonderful praise, because he published as many books as any one of us could scarcely copy, others' books, in his own hand.
passages.notes: The stray 'o' is a footnote mark. Read 'innumerabiles' for 'ipnumerabiles'. 'uosurum' is corrupt, presumably for 'nostrum' ('of us'). Chalcenterus is the nickname of Didymus.

passages.original: . Chartarum e usum primum Ægyptus ministravit cæptum apud Memphiticam urbem ; Memphis enim civitas Ægyptiorum est, ubi chartae usus inventus est primum, sicut ait Lucanus : Conficitur bibula Memphitis charta papyro. Bibulam autem papyrum dixit, quod humorem bibat.
passages.english: Egypt first supplied the use of papyrus sheets, beginning at the city of Memphis; for Memphis is a city of the Egyptians, where the use of papyrus sheets was first invented, as Lucan says: "The Memphite sheet is made from the thirsty papyrus." He called the papyrus "thirsty" because it drinks up moisture.
passages.notes: "charta" here means papyrus writing-sheet. The stray "e" after Chartarum is likely a footnote mark.

passages.original: 4. Membrana autem aut candida, aut lutea, aut purpurea sunt. Candida naturaliter existunt. Luteum membranum bicolor est, quod a confectore una tingitur parte, id est crocatur, de quo Persius : Jam liber, et positis bicolor membrana capillis.
passages.english: Parchments are either white, yellow or purple. White ones exist naturally. Yellow parchment is two-coloured, because it is dyed by the maker on one side, that is, coloured with saffron; of which Persius [says]: "Now the book, and the two-coloured parchment with its hair removed."

passages.original: 3. Circumcidi libros Siciliæ primum increbuit. Nam initio pumicabantur. Unde et ait Catullus : Cui dono lepidum novum libellum Arido modo pumice expolitum ?
passages.english: The trimming of books first became common in Sicily. For at first they were smoothed with pumice. Hence Catullus too says: "To whom do I give my charming new little book, just now polished with dry pumice?"
passages.notes: "Siciliæ" may mean "in Sicily"; the construction is loose.

passages.original: 3. Liber est interior tunica corticis quae ligno cohæret. De quo Virgilius : Alta liberaret in ulmo. Unde et liber dicitur in quo scrihimus, quia c ante usum chartae vel membranorum de libris arborum volumina fiebant, id est, compaginabantur. Unde et scriptores a libris arborum librarios vocaverunt.
passages.english: 3. The *liber* is the inner layer of the bark, which clings to the wood. Of this Virgil says: "He was stripping the bark (*liber*) on a lofty elm." Hence the thing in which we write is also called a *liber* [book], because before the use of papyrus or parchment, volumes were made, that is, bound together, from the barks (*libri*) of trees. Hence too they called scribes *librarii*, from the barks of trees.
passages.notes: "liberaret" appears to be a corruption; the Virgilian line (Eclogue 10.67) reads "aret" ("is withering") rather than "stripping"; the sense of the quotation is uncertain as printed. "scrihimus" read as "scribimus"; the stray "c" is a footnote mark.

passages.original: 4. Adam, sicut beatus Hieronymus tradidit, homo, sive terrenus, sive terra rubra interpretatur. Ex terra enim facta est caro, et humus hominis faciendi materies fuit.
passages.english: 4. Adam, as the blessed Jerome has handed down, is interpreted "man," or "earthly," or "red earth." For flesh was made from earth, and soil was the material from which man was to be made.

passages.original: 350 7. Lucretius autem superstitionem dicit superstantium rerum, id est, cœlestium et divinarum, quæ super nos stant, sed male dicit. Hæreticorum autem dogmata, ut facile possint agnosci, causas eorum vel nomina demonstrare oportuit.
passages.english: 7. Lucretius, however, says that superstition is [so called] from things standing above (*superstantes*), that is, heavenly and divine things, which stand above us; but he speaks wrongly. Now, so that the doctrines of the heretics may be easily recognized, it has been necessary to show their causes or names.
passages.notes: "350" is a page number of the printed edition.

passages.original: 40. i Origeniani ab Origene auctore exorti sunt, dicentes quod non possit Filius videre Patrem, nec Spiritus sanctus Filium. Animas quoque in mundi principio dicunt peecasse, et, pro diversitate peccatorum, a coelis usque ad terras diversa corpora, quasi vincula, meruisse, eaque causa factum fuisse mundum.
passages.english: 40. The Origenians arose from Origen as their founder, saying that the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son. They also say that souls sinned at the beginning of the world, and that, according to the diversity of their sins, they deserved different bodies, as if chains, ranging from the heavens down to the earth, and that for this reason the world was made.

passages.original: quorum varia constat opinio, quid Deus esset, dum quaererent. Quidam enim corporeo sensu hunc mundum visibilem ex quatuor elementis Deum esse dixerunt, 364 ut Dionysius Stoicus. Alii vero spiritualiter intellexerunt mentem esse Deum, ut Thales Milesius.
passages.english: Their opinion was varied, as they inquired what God was. For some, with a bodily understanding, said that this visible world, made of the four elements, is God, as Dionysius the Stoic [did]. Others, however, understood spiritually that God is mind, as Thales of Miletus [did].
passages.notes: "364" is a page number of the printed edition.

passages.original: 19. Quidam animum in omnibus commeantem, et b lucidum, ut Pythagoras. Quidam Deum sine tempore incommutabilem , ut Plato. Quidam mentem solutam, ut Cicero. Quidam , et spiritum, et mentem ut Maro. c Inventum enim solummodo Deum non, ut invenerunt, exposuerunt, quia evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis; dicentes enim se esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt.
passages.english: 19. Some [said God was] a spirit passing through all things, and shining, as Pythagoras [did]. Some [said God was] timeless and unchangeable, as Plato. Some [said he was] a mind set free, as Cicero. Some [said he was] both spirit and mind, as Maro [Virgil]. For having found God only, they did not set him forth as they had found him, because they became vain in their thoughts; for, claiming to be wise, they became fools.
passages.notes: The letters "b" and "c" are footnote marks. The sentence "Inventum enim solummodo Deum..." is awkward and may be corrupt; translated literally.

passages.original: 21. Unde et Varro ignem mundi animum dicit, prOinde quod in mundo ignis omnia gubernet, sicut animus in nobis. Quam vanissime : Qui eum est, inquit, in nobis, ipsi sumus ; cum exit, emorimur. Ergo, et e ignis cum de mundo per fulgura proficiscitur, mundus emoritur.
passages.english: Hence Varro also says that fire is the soul of the world, because in the world fire governs all things, just as the soul does in us. Most foolishly [he says]: "When it is in us," he says, "we ourselves exist; when it leaves, we die. Therefore, when fire departs from the world through lightning, the world dies."
passages.notes: Read 'Qui cum est' for 'Qui eum est'. The stray 'e' is a footnote mark. It is uncertain whether the last sentence continues the quotation from Varro or is the author's mocking inference from it.

passages.original: 22. Hi f philosophorum errores etiam apud Ecclesiam induxerunt hæreses. Inde αἰω̃νες, et formæ, nescioquæ, inde apud Arium Trinitas nominis, et apud Valentinum g Platonicus furor.
passages.english: These errors of the philosophers have also brought heresies into the Church. From them [come] the aeons, and forms, I know not what; from them, in Arius, a Trinity [only] in name, and in Valentinus the Platonic madness.
passages.notes: The stray letters 'f' and 'g' are footnote marks. 'Trinitas nominis' is an obscure phrase; it is taken to mean 'a Trinity in name only'.

passages.original: b. Tragici dicti, quod initio canentibus præmium erat hircus, quem Græci τράγον vocant. Unde et Horatius : Carmine, qui tragico vitem certavit ob hircum. Jam dehinc sequentes tragici multum honorem adepti sunt, excellentes in argumentis fabularum ad veritatis imaginem fictis.
passages.english: Tragedians were so called because at the beginning the prize for those who sang was a he-goat, which the Greeks call *tragos*. Hence Horace too: "He who in tragic song competed for a paltry goat." Then the tragedians who followed gained great honour, excelling in the plots of their stories, fashioned in the likeness of truth.
passages.notes: The initial "b." is likely a section or footnote mark. "vitem" read as "vilem" ("paltry"), as in Horace, Ars Poetica 220.

passages.original: a Duo sunt autem genera comicorum, id est, veteres et novi. 367 Veteres, qui et joco ridiculares exstiterunt, at Plautus, Actius, Terendus. Novi, qui et Satyrici a quibus generaliter vitia carpuntur, ut FlacCus, Persius, Juvenalis, et alii; hi enim universorum delicta corripiant; nec vetabatur eis pessimum quemque describere, nec cujuslibet peccata moresque reprehendere. Unde et nudi pinsuntur, eo quod per eos vitia singula denudentur.
passages.english: There are two kinds of comic writers, that is, the old and the new. The old, who were also laughable in their jesting, such as Plautus, Accius, Terence. The new, who are also called satirists, by whom vices are generally censured, such as Flaccus [Horace], Persius, Juvenal and others; for these rebuke the faults of all, and they were not forbidden to portray any wicked person, nor to reprove the sins and morals of anyone. Hence they are also painted naked, because through them individual vices are laid bare.
passages.notes: The initial "a" is a footnote mark; "367" is a page number. Read "ut" for "at", "Terentius" for "Terendus", "pinguntur" for "pinsuntur". "Actius" (Accius) as a comic poet is odd, but translated as printed.

passages.original: 11. f Apud poetas autem tres characteres sunt dicendi: unus in quo tantum poeta loquitur, ut est in libris Virgilii Georgicorum. Alius dramaticus, in quo nusquam poeta loquitur, ut est in comœdiis et tragœdiis. Tertius misius, ut est in Æneide. Nam poeta illic et introductae personae loquuntur.
passages.english: 11. Among poets there are three modes of speaking: one in which only the poet speaks, as in Virgil's books of the Georgics. Another, dramatic, in which the poet nowhere speaks, as in comedies and tragedies. The third, mixed, as in the Aeneid. For there both the poet and the characters introduced speak.
passages.notes: "f" is a footnote mark; "misius" read as "mixtus".

passages.original: 5. Septiina Cumana nomine Amalthæa, quæ novem libros attulit Tarquinio Prisco, k in quibus erant decreta Romana conscripta. Ipsa est et Cumaea, de qua Virgilius : Ultima Cumaei venit jam carminis ætas. 369 Dicta autem Cumana a civitate Cumis, quae est in Campania, cujus sepulcrum in Sicilia adhuc manet.
passages.english: 5. The seventh, the Cumaean, named Amalthea, who brought nine books to Tarquinius Priscus, in which Roman decrees were written down. She is also the Cumaean of whom Virgil [says]: "Now has come the last age of the Cumaean song." She was called Cumaean from the city of Cumae, which is in Campania; her tomb still remains in Sicily.
passages.notes: "Septiina" read as "Septima"; "k" is a footnote mark; "369" is a page number.

passages.original: 1. Magorum 1 primus Zoroastes rex Bactrianorum, quem Ninus rex Assyriorum praelio interfecit.dem quo Aristoteles scribit quod vicies centum millia versuum ab ipso condita indiciis volaminum ejus declarentur.
passages.english: The first of the magi was Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, whom Ninus, king of the Assyrians, killed in battle. Aristotle writes of him that two million verses composed by him are attested by the indexes of his volumes.
passages.notes: "interfecit.dem quo" read as "interfecit. De quo"; "volaminum" read as "voluminum". "Magorum 1": stray footnote mark omitted.

passages.original: i. Hanc artem multa post sæcula Democritus ampliavit, quando et Hippocrates medicinæ disciplina effloruit. Apud Assyrios autem magicae artes copiosa sunt, testante Lucano : .... qais noscere fibra FaLa queat. quis prodat aves, quis fulgura cœli Servet et Assyria scrutetur sidera cura.
passages.english: Many centuries later Democritus expanded this art, at the time when Hippocrates also flourished in the discipline of medicine. Among the Assyrians, moreover, the magic arts are abundant, as Lucan testifies: "... who could know the fates from entrails, who could interpret birds, who could observe the lightnings of the sky and examine the stars with Assyrian care."
passages.notes: "qais ... FaLa" read as "quis ... fata". Leading "i." appears to be a section number or scanning residue.

passages.original: 10. Unde et Lucanus : Mens hausti nulla sanie polluta veneni r Incantata perit. Dæmonibus enim accitis, 's audent ventilare, ut quisque suos perimat malis artibus inimicos. Hi h etiam sanguine utuntur, et victimis, et saepe contingunt , corpora mortuorum.
passages.english: Hence also Lucan: "A mind polluted by no gore of swallowed poison perishes, enchanted." For, having summoned demons, they dare to stir [them] up, so that each may destroy his enemies by evil arts. These also make use of blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the dead.
passages.notes: Stray letters (r, 's, h) omitted. "ventilare" ('to stir up, toss about') is obscure here; the object is implied.

passages.original: 13. Quod genus divinationis a 1 Persis dicitur al- latum. Varro dicit divinationis quatuor esse genera, terram, aquam, aerem, ignem. Hinc geomantiam, hydromantiam, aeromantiam, pyromantiam'
passages.english: 13. This kind of divination is said to have been brought from the Persians. Varro says that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, fire. Hence geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, pyromancy.

passages.original: 40. 1 Unde etiam Homerus dicit eum præcipitatum de aere in terras, 383 quod omne fulmen de acre cadit. m Idcirco autem Vulcanus de femore Junonis finitur natus, quod fulmina de imo aere nascuntur.
passages.english: Hence Homer also says that he was thrown down from the air to the earth, because every thunderbolt falls from the air. And Vulcan is feigned to have been born from Juno's thigh for this reason, that thunderbolts are born from the lowest air.
passages.notes: "acre" read as "aere"; "finitur" read as "fingitur". Stray marks (1, 383, m) omitted.

passages.original: 48. Nam bellantes ac dissidentes interpretum oratione sedantur; unde et secundum Livium legati pacis caduceatores dicuntur. Sicut enim per faeciales bella Indicebantur, ita pax per caduceatores fiebat.
passages.english: For those at war and in dispute are calmed by the speech of intermediaries; hence also, according to Livy, envoys of peace are called caduceatores [bearers of the herald's staff]. For just as wars were declared through the fetials, so peace was made through the caduceatores.
passages.notes: "faeciales" = fetiales, the Roman priests who declared war.

passages.original: 57. Ipsam et LuMnam asseverant, eo quod luceat. Eamdem et Triviam, quod tribus fingatur figuris. D6 qua Virgilius : .... Tria virginis ora Dianæ, 1 quia ea. dem Luna, eadem Diana, eadem Proserpina vocatur.
passages.english: They also declare her to be the Moon (Luna), because she shines (luceat). [They call] her also Trivia, because she is represented with three forms. Of her Virgil [says]: "... the three faces of the maiden Diana," because the same [goddess] is called Luna, Diana and Proserpina.
passages.notes: "LuMnam" read as "Lunam"; "D6 qua" as "De qua".

passages.original: r 63. Massagetæ ex Scytharum origine sunt. Et dicti Massagetæ, quasi graves, id esi, forte Getæ. h Nam sic Livius argentum grave dicit, id est, massas. Hi sunt qui inter Scytbas atque Albanos septentrionalibus jugis inhabitant.
passages.english: The Massagetae are of Scythian origin. And they are called Massagetae as if 'heavy', that is, 'strong' Getae. For thus Livy speaks of 'heavy silver', that is, masses (massae). These are the ones who dwell in the northern ranges between the Scythians and the Albanians.
passages.notes: Stray marks (r, h) omitted.

passages.original: 74. Peiasgi nominati quia cum velis passis verno tempore advenisse italiam b visi sunt, ut aves. c Primos enim eos Varro Italiam appulisse commemorat. Græci vero Pelasgos a Pelasgo, Jovis et Larissæ filio, perhibent dictos.
passages.english: 74. The Pelasgians were so named because they were seen to have arrived in Italy in springtime with sails spread, like birds. For Varro records that they were the first to land in Italy. The Greeks, however, hold that they were called Pelasgians after Pelasgus, the son of Jupiter and Larissa.
passages.notes: 'Peiasgi' read as 'Pelasgi'. The etymology implied is from Greek pelargos, 'stork'.

passages.original: 75. a Myrmidone. fuerunt Achillis socii; Dolopes Pyrrhi, dicti autem Myrmidones propter astutiam, quasi μύρμηϰες, id est, formicæ. Eratosthenes autem dicit dictos Myrmidones a Myrmidone duce, Jovis et Eurimedusae, filio
passages.english: 75. From Myrmidon. The Myrmidons were the companions of Achilles; the Dolopes [those] of Pyrrhus; and they were called Myrmidons on account of their cunning, as if *myrmēkes*, that is, ants. But Eratosthenes says the Myrmidons were named from their leader Myrmidon, son of Jupiter and Eurymedusa.
passages.notes: The opening 'a Myrmidone' appears to be a heading or fragment; the sense of the first sentence is somewhat garbled.

passages.original: Saevissimi enim omnium gentium fuerunt; unde et wulta de eis fabulosa memorantur : quod captivos diis suis litarent, et huma- i num sanguinem in ossibus capitum essem soliti potare. De quibus Virgilius : Heu fuge crudeles terras, fuge littus avarum, quasi crudelium et avarorum
passages.english: For they were the most savage of all nations; hence many fabulous things are also related about them: that they sacrificed captives to their gods and were accustomed to drink human blood from the bones of skulls. Of them Virgil [says]: "Alas, flee the cruel lands, flee the greedy shore," as if [the shore] of the cruel and greedy
passages.notes: "essem" read as "eorum" or similar; stray "i" omitted. The passage breaks off mid-sentence.

passages.original: Gothi a Magog filio Japhet nominati pusantur, de similitudine ultimae syllabae, quos veteres magis Getas quam Gothos vocaverunt, gens fortis et potentissima, rorporum mole ardua, armorum genere terribilis, de quibus Lucanus : Hinc Dacus premat, inde Getes occurrat. Iberis.
passages.english: The Goths are thought to have been named from Magog, son of Japheth, from the likeness of the final syllable; the ancients called them Getae rather than Goths. [They are] a brave and most powerful people, lofty in the bulk of their bodies, terrible in the kind of their arms, of whom Lucan [says]: "Let the Dacian press from here, the Getan rush against [us] from there." Iberians.
passages.notes: "pusantur" read as "putantur"; "rorporum" as "corporum". The final word "Iberis" appears to be the heading of the next entry (on the Iberians) and stands apart from the sentence.

passages.original: 94. Lanus fluvius fertur ultra Danubium, a quo Alani dicti sunt, d sicut et populi inhabitantes juxta Lemannum fluvium Alemani vocantur. De qui- bus Lucanus : Deseruere cavo tentoria fixa Lemanno.
passages.english: The Lanus is said to be a river beyond the Danube, from which the Alani are named, just as the peoples living beside the river Lemannus are called Alemanni. Of them Lucan [says]: "They have deserted the tents pitched by the deep Lemannus."
passages.notes: Lemannus is properly Lake Geneva (Leman), which Isidore treats as a river.

passages.original: 98. Suevi pars Germanorum fuerunt iu fine Sep. tentrionis; de quibus Lucanus : Fundit ab extremo flavos Aquilone Suevos Quorum fuisse centum pagos et populos multi prodiderunt. Dicti autem Suevi putantur a monte Suevo, qui ab ortu initium Germaniæ facit, cujusloca incoluerunt.
passages.english: The Suevi were a part of the Germans at the edge of the North; of them Lucan [says]: "He pours forth the blond Suevi from the farthest North." Many have recorded that they had a hundred districts and peoples. The Suevi are thought to be named from Mount Suevus, which forms the beginning of Germany on the east, whose regions they inhabited.

passages.original: 102. Britones quidam Latlne nominatos suspicantur, eo quod bruti sint, gens inter Oceanum, inlerfuso mari, quasi extra orbem posita. De quibus Virgilius : Toto divisos orbe Britannos.
passages.english: 102. Some suppose that the Britons were named in Latin because they are brutish (bruti), a people set within the Ocean, with the sea flowing between, as if placed outside the world. Of them Virgil [says]: "The Britons, divided from the whole world."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "Latlne" for Latine, "inlerfuso" for interfuso.

passages.original: 123. i Massylia civitas Africæ est, non longe ab Atlante, et hortis Hesperidum ; a qua civitate Missylii vocati sunt, quos nos corrupte Massulos vocamus, de quibus Virgilius : Hinc mihi Massylæ gentis monstrata sacerdos.
passages.english: 123. Massylia is a city of Africa, not far from Atlas and the gardens of the Hesperides; from this city the Massylii are named, whom we, by corruption, call Massuli. Of them Virgil [says]: "From there a priestess of the Massylian race was shown to me."
passages.notes: Initial "i" taken as a footnote mark. "Missylii" read as Massylii.

passages.original: 13. Julius autem dictus, quia ab Iulo Æneæ filio, originem duxit, ut confirmat Virgilius : Julius a magno demissum nomen Iulo.
passages.english: 13. And Julius was so called because he drew his origin from Iulus, the son of Aeneas, as Virgil confirms: "Julius, a name handed down from great Iulus."

passages.original: 37. h Romanae autem militiæ mos fuit puberes primo exerceri armis. Nam decimo sexto anno tirones militabant. quo etiam solo sub custodibus agebaut, de quibus Virgilius : Et primævo flore juventus.
passages.english: 37. It was the custom of Roman military service that youths were first trained in arms. For at the sixteenth year recruits served as soldiers; and in that year alone they lived under guardians. Of them Virgil [says]: "And the youth in its first flower."
passages.notes: Initial "h" taken as a footnote mark; "agebaut" read as agebant.

passages.original: manipuli autem dicti sunt milites, sive quia bellum primo manu incipiebant, sive quod antequam signa essent manipulos sibi, id est, fasciculos stipulæ, vel herbae alicujus, pro signis faciebant, a quo signo maniputares milites cognominati sunt. De quibus Lucanus : Convocat armatos extemplo ad signa maniplos.
passages.english: And soldiers were called maniples, either because they first began battle by hand (manu), or because, before there were standards, they made for themselves maniples, that is, small bundles of straw or of some plant, to serve as standards; from this standard the soldiers were surnamed manipulares. Of them Lucan [says]: "At once he calls the armed maniples together to the standards."
passages.notes: "maniputares" read as manipulares.

passages.original: 59. Classes dictae propter divisionem exercitus, qui postea manipuli dicti sunt. Unde et Virgilius: Classibus hic locus, hic acies certare solebant. Jam postea et classis navium dicta.
passages.english: 59. Classes (classes) were so called on account of the division of the army; these were later called maniples. Hence Virgil also [says]: "Here was the place for the classes, here the battle lines used to contend." And afterwards a fleet of ships was also called a classis.

passages.original: 64. h Agmen dicitur cum exercitus iter facit, ab agendo vocatum, id est, eundo. Plautus : Quo te agis ipse? Est enim exercitus ambulans. Nam agmen dicitur quod in longitudine directum est, quale solet esse cum exercitus portis procedit; quidquid fuerit aliud, abusive dicitur.
passages.english: 64. An agmen is spoken of when an army is on the march; it is named from agere, that is, going. Plautus: "Where are you taking yourself?" For it is an army walking. For agmen is said of what is drawn out in length, such as it usually is when an army proceeds out of the gates; anything else is so called by misuse.
passages.notes: Initial "h" taken as a footnote mark.

passages.original: 10. g Patres autem, Ut dicit Sallustius, a curæ similitudine votati sunt. Nam sicut patres filios suos, ita illi h rempublicam habebant.
passages.english: 10. And the Fathers, as Sallust says, were so called from the likeness of their care. For as fathers [hold] their sons, so they held the commonwealth.
passages.notes: Stray "g" and "h" taken as footnote marks; "votati" read as vocati.

passages.original: 33. d Villicus proprie villæ gubernator est. Unde et a villa VILLICUS nomen accepit. Interdum autcm villicus non gubernationem vilæ, sed dispensationem univer- Sae domus, Tullio interpretante, significat, quod est universarum possessionum et villarum dispensatorem.
passages.english: 33. A villicus is properly the manager of a villa (country estate). Hence the villicus took his name from villa. Sometimes, however, villicus signifies not the management of a villa but the stewardship of the whole household, as Tully interprets it, that is, the steward of all the possessions and villas.
passages.notes: Initial "d" taken as a footnote mark.

passages.original: 28. b In eligendo marito quatuor spectari solent: virtus,genus, pulchritudo, sapientia. Ex his sapien: tia potentior est ad amoris affectum. Refert hæc quatuor Virgilius de Ænea, quod bis Dido impulsa est in tamorem ejus. Pulchritudine : Quem sese ore ferens Virtute : Quam forti pectore, et armis. Oratione : ..... Heu! qoibus ille Jactatus fatis, quæ bella exhausta canebat! Genere : Credo equidem, nec vana fides, genas esse deorum.
passages.english: 28. In choosing a husband four things are usually looked to: virtue, birth, beauty, wisdom. Of these, wisdom is the more powerful in stirring the feeling of love. Virgil relates these four of Aeneas, by which Dido was driven into love of him. By beauty: "How he bears himself in his countenance!" By virtue: "How brave of heart, and in arms!" By speech: "Alas, by what fates he has been tossed! What wars endured to the end he was telling!" By birth: "I believe indeed, and it is no vain belief, that he is of the race of the gods."
passages.notes: "bis" read as his ("by which"); "tamorem" as amorem; "genas" as genus. The list names "wisdom" but the example is labelled "speech" (oratione). The ellipsis is in the edition.

passages.original: 62. Convulsus dicitur, cui sua, vi aliqua adimuntur. Unde et convutsa navis, cujus eminentia vi tempestatis adimuntur; unde et Virgilius : Vix saptem canvulsæ undis, quasi mutilatæ.
passages.english: 62. A person is called *convulsus* [torn away] from whom his own things are taken away by some force. Hence also a *convulsa* ship, whose projecting parts are taken away by the force of a storm; hence also Virgil: "Scarcely seven, torn by the waves," as if mutilated.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'convutsa' for 'convulsa', 'saptem canvulsæ' for 'septem convulsæ'. The Latin 'sua' (his own things) is plural while 'adimuntur' agrees; the sense is clear.

passages.original: Fornicatrix est cujus corpus publicum et valgare est. Hæ sub arcuatis prostabant, quæ loca fornices dicuntur; unde et fornicariæ. Virgilius : Atque adverso fornice.
passages.english: A *fornicatrix* [prostitute] is one whose body is public and common. These women used to stand for hire under arched structures, places which are called *fornices* [arches]; hence also [they are called] *fornicariae*. Virgil: "And from the opposite arch."
passages.notes: 'valgare' read as 'vulgare'.

passages.original: d Locuples, quasi loci. plenus, et possessionum plurimarum possessor, quemadmodum ducet Tullius n libro II, de Republica : c Multaque dilione ovium « et boum, quod tunc res erat in pecore, et in loco. rum possessionibus ; ex quo pecuniosi et locu. pleles vocabantur. »
passages.english: *Locuples* [wealthy], as if *loci plenus* [full of place], and the possessor of very many possessions, as Cicero says in book II of the Republic: "And by a great holding of sheep and cattle, because then wealth lay in livestock and in the possession of places; from which [people] were called *pecuniosi* [moneyed] and *locupletes* [wealthy]."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'ducet' for 'docet', 'n' for 'in', 'dilione' for 'ditione', 'locu. pleles' for 'locupletes'; stray letters 'd' and 'c' omitted as footnote marks. 'ditione' (holding, possession) is the likely reading.

passages.original: 174. e Miser proprie, eo quod omnem felicitatem amiserit. Secundum autem Ciceronem, proprie mortuus, qui in Tusculanis miseros mortuos vocat, propter quod jam amiserunt vitam.
passages.english: 174. *Miser* [wretched] properly [means one so called] because he has lost (*amiserit*) all happiness. But according to Cicero it properly [means] a dead man, since in the Tusculans he calls the dead *miseri*, because they have now lost life.

passages.original: 180. Metatores appellantur, qui castra designant, a metiendo, scilicet Lucanus : Hesperios audax veniat metator in agros.
passages.english: 180. Those who lay out a camp are called *metatores* [surveyors], from *metiendo* [measuring], as Lucan [says]: "Let the bold surveyor come into the Hesperian fields."

passages.original: 186. a Nihili, compositum est ex ne et hilo. Hilum nutem Varro ait significare medullam ejus ferulae quam Græci aspbodelon vocant; et sic dici apud nos nihilum ; quomodo apud Graecos οὺδέ γρυ̃.
passages.english: 186. Nihili ["of nothing"] is compounded from ne and hilum. Varro says that hilum means the pith of that fennel-stalk which the Greeks call asphodel; and that nihilum is said thus among us, just as among the Greeks [they say] oude gry ["not a whit"].
passages.notes: 'nutem' read as 'autem'; 'aspbodelon' as 'asphodelon'.

passages.original: 224. b Prævaricator, malae fide! advocatus, et qui, vel in accusando nocitura, vel in defendendo profutura praetereat,aut inutiliter491 dubiequeponat, mercedis gratia, scilicet corruptus. Cicero: Quid enim tam prævarum? id est, valde varum.
passages.english: 224. A *praevaricator* [collusive advocate] is an advocate of bad faith, one who, either in accusing passes over what would harm [the other side], or in defending passes over what would help [his client], or puts [it] forward uselessly and doubtfully, for the sake of a fee, that is, corrupted. Cicero: "For what is so crooked (*praevarum*)?" that is, very crooked (*varum*).
passages.notes: 'malae fide!' read as 'malae fidei'; the page number 491 in the text omitted. *Varus* means bow-legged, crooked.

passages.original: 234. Religiosus, h ait Cicero, a relegendo appellatur, qui retractat, et tanquam relegit ea quae ad cultum divinum pertineant. Hisunt dicti religiosi ex religendo, tanquam ex ELIGENDO eligentes, ex DILIGENDO diligentes ex INTELLGENDO intelligentes.
passages.english: 234. *Religiosus* [religious], Cicero says, is so called from *relegendo* [re-reading], [being one] who goes back over and as it were re-reads the things that pertain to divine worship. These are called *religiosi* from *religendo*, just as *eligentes* [choosers] from *eligendo*, *diligentes* [diligent] from *diligendo*, *intelligentes* [intelligent] from *intelligendo*.

passages.original: J Solers , quod sit sollicitus in arte, et utilis. Solers enim apud antiquos dicebatur, qui erat omni bona arte instructus. Terentius : Adolescentem solertem dabo.
passages.english: *Solers* [skilful], because he is careful in an art (*sollicitus in arte*), and useful. For among the ancients *solers* was used of one who was trained in every good art. Terence: "I will provide a skilful young man."
passages.notes: Initial 'J' omitted as a footnote mark.

passages.original: 244. e Superstitiosos ait Cicero appellatos qui totos dies precabantur, 494 et immolabant, ut sibi sui liberi superstites essent.
passages.english: 244. Cicero says that those were called *superstitiosi* [superstitious] who prayed and sacrificed for whole days so that their children might survive them (*superstites*).
passages.notes: Page number 494 omitted.

passages.original: Teter, ab obscura tenebrosaque vita. Teterrimus pro fero nimium. Tetrum enim veteres pro Fero diierunt, ut Ennius : Tetrosque elephantos.
passages.english: Teter ["foul"], from an obscure and shadowy life. Teterrimus [is used] for "exceedingly savage". For the ancients said tetrum for "savage", as Ennius: "and the foul elephants."
passages.notes: 'diierunt' read as 'dixerunt'.

passages.original: Versutus, eo quod ejus mens in quolibet acu ad quamlibet fraudem facile veriitur, unde et versutis dictur contorta sententis. Plautus : Versutior quam rota figularis.
passages.english: *Versutus* [wily], because his mind is easily turned (*vertitur*), in any matter whatever, to any fraud whatever; hence also a twisted statement is called *versuta*. Plautus: "More wily (*versutior*) than a potter's wheel."
passages.notes: 'acu' probably for 'actu' (matter, action); 'versutis dictur contorta sententis' read as 'versuta dicitur contorta sententia'.

passages.original: 5. d Iam proprie homo ab humo. * Graeci autem hominem ἄνθρωπον appellaverunt, 2 eo quod sursum spectet, sublevatus ab humo ad contemplationem ar. titicis sui. Quod Ovidius poeta designat, cum dicit: Pronaque cum spectent aaimalia caetera terram, Os homini sublime dedit, cœlumque videre Jussit, et erectos ad sidera tollere vultus. Qui ideo erectus coelum aspicit, ut Deum quaerat, non ut terram intendat, f veluti pecora, quæ natura prona et ventri obedientia finxit.
passages.english: Now, properly, "man" (homo) [is named] from "earth" (humus). The Greeks, however, called man anthrōpos, because he looks upward, raised up from the earth to the contemplation of his maker. This is what the poet Ovid points to when he says: "And while the other animals bend down and look at the earth, he gave man a lofty face, and bade him see the sky and lift his upright countenance to the stars." Man therefore stands upright and looks at the sky so that he may seek God, not so that he may fix [his gaze] on the earth, like the beasts, which nature has shaped bent down and obedient to the belly.
passages.notes: The stray letters 'd', '2' and 'f' are footnote marks and are omitted. 'ar. titicis' is read as 'artificis' (maker) and 'aaimalia' as 'animalia'.

passages.original: d Nares idcirco nominantur, quia per eas, vel odor, vel spiritus nare non desinit; sive e quia nos odore admonent, ut norimus aliquid, 9 et sciamus ; unde e contra inscii ac rudes ignari dicuntur. Olfecisse enim , veteres scisse dicebant. Terentius : Ac non totis sex mensibus prius offecissem, quam ille quidquam cæperet.
passages.english: The nostrils (nares) are so named because through them either smell or breath does not cease to flow (nare); or else because they prompt us by smell, so that we may know (norimus) something and be aware of it; hence, on the contrary, the unknowing and uncultivated are called ignorant (ignari). For the ancients used to say "to have smelled out" for "to have known." Terence: "And would I not have smelled it out a full six months earlier, before he had begun anything."
passages.notes: The stray letters 'd', 'e' and '9' are footnote marks and are omitted. 'offecissem' is read as 'olfecissem' and 'cæperet' as 'caperet'. The Terence quotation is loosely rendered by Isidore.

passages.original: 51. Linguæ a 1 ligando cibum putat Varro nomen impositum. Alii quod per articulatos sonos verba ligat. J Sicut enim plectrum cordis, ita lingua illidilur dentibus, et vocalem efficit sciram.
passages.english: 51. Varro thinks that the name lingua ["tongue"] was given from ligare ["binding"] food. Others [say it is] because it binds words through articulated sounds. For just as the plectrum [strikes] the strings, so the tongue is struck against the teeth and produces vocal sound.
