passages.notes: 'illidilur' read as 'illiditur'; 'sciram' is evidently corrupt, probably for 'sonum' (sound).

passages.original: 67. Dextra vocatur a dando, ipsa enim pignus pacis datur, ipsa P fidei testis atque salutis adhibetur, et hoc est illud apud Tullium : Fidem publicam jussu senatus dedi, id est, dextram. Unde et Apostolus : Dextras dederunt, mihi et Barnabæ, societatis.
passages.english: The right hand (dextra) is named from giving (dando), for it is given as a pledge of peace, and it is used as a witness of faith and of safety. This is what is meant in Tully: "By order of the senate I gave the public faith," that is, the right hand. Hence also the Apostle: "They gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas."
passages.notes: The stray 'P' is a footnote mark and is omitted.

passages.original: 97. f Renes, ait Varro, dictos, quod rivi ab bis obsceni humoris nascantur. Nam venæ et medullae tenuem liquorem desudant in renibus, qui liquor rursus a renibus calore venereo resolutus decurrit.
passages.english: 97. The kidneys (renes), says Varro, are so called because streams (rivi) of obscene fluid arise from them. For the veins and marrow exude a thin liquid into the kidneys, and this liquid, released again by sexual heat, flows down from the kidneys.

passages.original: 109. Denique complicatum gigni formarique hominem (dicunt) ita ut genua sursum sint, quibus oculi formantur, ut cavi, ac reconditi fiant. Ennius :
passages.english: 109. Finally, they say that a human being is conceived and formed folded up, so that the knees are upward, by which the eyes are shaped, so that they become hollow and deep-set. Ennius:
passages.notes: The quotation from Ennius is not included in the passage.

passages.original: 133. Alvus est, quæ cibum recipit, et purgari solet. Sallustius : S mulans sibi alvum purgari. Et vocatur alvus, quod abluatur, id est, purgetur. Ex ipsa enim sordes stercorum defluunt
passages.english: The belly (alvus) is that which receives food and is regularly purged. Sallust: "pretending that his bowels were being purged." And it is called alvus because it is washed out (abluatur), that is, purged. For from it the filth of excrement flows away.
passages.notes: 'S mulans' is read as 'simulans' (pretending).

passages.original: 1. Portenta o esse ait Varro, quae contra naturam nata videntur; sed non sunt contra naturam, quia divina voluntate fiunt, cum voluntas Crealoris cujusque conditæ rei natura sit. Unde et ipsi gentiles Deum modo Naturam, modo Deum appellant.
passages.english: 1. Varro says that portents are things which appear to have been born contrary to nature; but they are not contrary to nature, because they come about by divine will, since the will of the Creator is the nature of every created thing. Hence the pagans themselves call God sometimes Nature, sometimes God.

passages.original: 7. Exempli causa, cum ex digitis nati. Portenla igitur, vel portentosa, existunt, alia magniludine totius corporis ultra communem hominum modum, h quantus fuit Tityon in novem jugeribus jacens. i Homero testante; alia, parvitate totius corporis, ut nani, vel quos Græci pygmaeos vocant, eo quod sint statura cubitales ; alii magnitudine partium, veluti capite informi, aut superfluis membrorum partibus, ut biciptes, et trimani, i vel cynodontes, quibus gemini procedunt dentes.
passages.english: For example, when [people] are born with [extra] fingers. Portents, then, or portentous [beings], appear: some through the size of the whole body beyond the common measure of humans, as great as Tityos was, lying over nine iugera, as Homer testifies; others through the smallness of the whole body, like dwarfs, or those whom the Greeks call Pygmies, because they are a cubit tall; others through the size of parts, such as a misshapen head, or through superfluous parts of the limbs, like the two-headed and the three-handed, or the cynodontes ["dog-toothed"], in whom double teeth protrude.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is a fragment from the preceding text. Stray 'h' and 'i' are footnote marks; 'Portenla', 'magniludine' and 'biciptes' are read as 'portenta', 'magnitudine' and 'bicipites'. A iugerum is a Roman land measure.

passages.original: Alia, quae ex omni parte transfigurantur in alienae creationis portentum, ut ex muliere vitu- lum dicit historia generatum. Alia, quae sine transfiguratione mutationem habent locorum, ut oculos in pectore, vel in fronte, aures supra tempora, vel sicut Aristoteles tradidit, quemdam in sinistra parte jecur, in dextera splenem habuisse.
passages.english: Others are wholly transformed into a portent of another kind of creature, as history says a calf was born from a woman. Others, without transformation, have a change in the position [of their parts], such as eyes in the chest or on the forehead, or ears above the temples, or, as Aristotle reported, a certain man who had his liver on the left side and his spleen on the right.

passages.original: 35. Nam hydra ab aqua dicla est. c llujus mentionem facit Ambrosius in similitudinem hæresium, dicens : Hæresis enim, velut quædam hydra fabularum, vulneribus suis crevit; et dum sæpe reciditur, pullulat, igni debita, incendioque peritura.
passages.english: For the hydra is named from water. Ambrose mentions it as a likeness of heresies, saying: "For heresy, like a sort of hydra of the fables, has grown by its wounds; and while it is often cut back, it sprouts again, destined for the fire and doomed to perish by burning."
passages.notes: The stray 'c' is a footnote mark and is omitted; 'llujus' is read as 'Hujus'.

passages.original: 38. Porro Minotaurum nomen sumpsisse ex tanro et homine, qualem bestiam dicunt fabulose in Labyrintho inclusam fuisse. De qua Ovidius : Semibovemque virum, semivirumque bovem.
passages.english: Further, [they say that] the Minotaur took its name from bull (taurus) and man, the sort of beast they tell in fables was shut up in the Labyrinth. Of it Ovid [says]: "a half-bull man and a half-man bull."
passages.notes: The infinitive 'sumpsisse' implies an omitted verb of saying. 'tanro' is read as 'tauro'.

passages.original: Siquidem et per naturam pleraque mutationem recipiunt, et corrupta in diversas species transformantur, sicut de vitulorum carnibus putridis apes, sicut de equis scarabci, de mulis locustæ, de cancris scorpioncs. Ovidius : Concava littorei si demas brachia cancri, Scorpius exibit, caudaque minabitur unca.
passages.english: Indeed, many things also undergo change by nature, and when decayed are transformed into different species, as bees [come] from the rotting flesh of calves, beetles from horses, locusts from mules, scorpions from crabs. Ovid: "If you remove the hollow claws of a shore crab, a scorpion will emerge and threaten with its hooked tail."
passages.notes: 'scarabci' and 'scorpioncs' are read as 'scarabei' and 'scorpiones'.

passages.original: 14. Hircus, lascivum anima!, et petulcum, ct fervens semper ad coitum, cujus oculi ob libidinem in transversum aspiciunt, unde et nomen traxit. n Nam hirqui sunt oculorum anguli secundum Suetonium, cujus natura adeo calidissima est, ut adamantem lapidem, quem nec ignis, nec ferri domare valet materia, solus hujus cruor dissolvat. 0 Majores hirci Ciniphii dicuntur a fluvio Ciniphe in Libya, ubi grandes nascuntur.i
passages.english: 14. The he-goat (hircus) is a lustful, butting animal, always burning for copulation, whose eyes from lust look sideways, whence it also took its name. For according to Suetonius the corners of the eyes are called hirqui. Its nature is so extremely hot that its blood alone dissolves the adamant stone, which neither fire nor iron can subdue. Larger he-goats are called Cinyphian, from the river Cinyps in Libya, where large ones are born.
passages.notes: Stray marks (n, 0, i) are footnote signs, omitted.

passages.original: 42. 22. Damula vocata , quod de manu effugiat : timidum animal et imbelie ; de quo Martialis : Dente timetur aper, defendunt cornua cervum. Imbelles damæ, quid nisi præda sumus ?
passages.english: The fallow deer (damula) is so called because it flees from the hand (de manu): a timid and unwarlike animal. Of it Martial [says]: "The boar is feared for its tusk, horns defend the stag; we unwarlike deer, what are we but prey?"
passages.notes: The etymology plays on 'de manu'. 'imbelie' is read as 'imbelle'.

passages.original: I Porcus, quasi spurcus, Ingurgitat enim se cœno, luto immergit, limo illinit. Horatius : Et amica luto sus; hinc etiam spurcitia, vel spurcus, nuncupatur.
passages.english: The pig (porcus) is named as if 'filthy' (spurcus). For it gorges itself in muck, plunges into mud, and smears itself with slime. Horace: 'And the sow, friend of mud.' From this also filthiness (spurcitia), or filthy (spurcus), is named.
passages.notes: The initial 'I' is likely a stray section mark from the printed page and has been omitted.

passages.original: ° Circa hominem leonum natura est benigna, ut nisi læsi nequeant irasci. Patet enim eorum misericordia exemplis assiduis. Prostratis enim parount; p captivos obvios repalriare permittunt; hominem 52 non nisi in magna fame interimunt. De quibus Lucretius : Scymnique leonum, etc.
passages.english: Toward humans the nature of lions is kindly, so that unless they are injured they cannot become angry. Their mercy is evident from constant examples. For they spare those who lie prostrate; they allow captives they meet to return home; they do not kill a human except in great hunger. Of them Lucretius [says]: 'And the cubs of lions,' etc.
passages.notes: Read 'parcunt' for 'parount' and 'repatriare' for 'repalriare'; stray marks '°', 'p' and the page number '52' omitted.

passages.original: Itaque oneratam fetibus vulvam tanquam obstanlem partui unguibus laeerant, effundit illa partum, seu potius dimittit, dolore cogente. Ita postea corruptis et cicatricosis sedibus genitale semen infusum non hæret acceptum, sed irritum resilit. d Nam Plinius dicit animalia cum acutis unguibus frequenter parere non posse. Vitiantur enim intrinsceus se moventibus catnlis.
passages.english: And so they tear with their claws the womb laden with offspring, as though it obstructed the birth; she pours out the offspring, or rather lets it go, compelled by pain. Thus afterwards, the seats [of conception] being damaged and scarred, the generative seed poured in does not stay once received, but springs back without effect. For Pliny says that animals with sharp claws cannot give birth often, for they are injured by the cubs moving inside.
passages.notes: The animal (from earlier context) is the lioness. Stray letter "d" omitted.

passages.original: 11. Leopardus ex adulterio leænæ, et pardi nascitur, et tertiam originem efficit, sicut et Plinius in naturali historia dicit leonem eum parda, aut pardum cum leæna concumbere, et ex utroque coitu degeneres partus creari, d ut mulus et burdo.
passages.english: 11. The leopard is born from the adultery of a lioness and a pard, and makes a third kind, just as Pliny also says in the Natural History, that a lion mates with a female pard, or a pard with a lioness, and from either union degenerate offspring are produced, like the mule and the hinny.
passages.notes: Read 'cum' for 'eum'. 'Burdo' is the offspring of a stallion and a she-ass (hinny). Stray mark 'd' omitted.

passages.original: Hujus urinam converti in duritiam pretiosi lapidis dicun', qui c lincurius appellatur, quod et ipsos lynces sentire hoc documento probatur; nam egestum liquorem arenis, in quantum poluerint, contegunt, invidia quadam naturæ, ne talis egestio 56 transeat in usum humanum.d Lynces dicit Plinius secundus extra unum non admittere.
passages.english: They say that its urine is turned into the hardness of a precious stone, which is called lyncurius; and that lynxes themselves are aware of this is proved by this evidence: they cover the discharged liquid with sand as far as they can, out of a certain natural grudging, lest such a discharge pass into human use. Pliny the Second says that lynxes do not bear more than one [offspring].
passages.notes: Read 'dicunt' and 'potuerint'; stray marks 'c', 'd' and page number '56' omitted. 'Extra unum non admittere' is taken as 'bear no more than one young', as in Pliny.

passages.original: Nam testiculi eorum apti sunt medicaminibus, propter quod cum præsenserint venatorem, ipsi se castrant, et morsibus vires suas amputant. De quibns Cicero in Scauriana : Redimunt se ea parte corpori propter quam maxime expetuntur. Juvenalis : qui se Eunuchum ipse facit cupiens evadere damno Testiculi. Ipsi sunt et fibri, qui etiam pontici canes vocantur.
passages.english: For their testicles are suitable for medicines; because of this, when they sense a hunter in advance, they castrate themselves and cut off their potency with their bites. Of them Cicero in the Pro Scauro [says]: 'They ransom themselves with that part of the body for which they are most sought.' Juvenal: '[like the beaver] who makes himself a eunuch, wishing to escape by the loss of a testicle.' They are also the fibri, which are also called Pontic dogs.
passages.notes: Read 'quibus' and 'corporis'. The context gives the etymology of castor from castrare (garbled in the scan).

passages.original: 28. a Lycisci autem dicuntur, ut ait Plinius, canes nati ex lupis et canihus, cum inter se forte miscentur. p Solent et Indæ feminæ canes noctu in silvis alligtæ admitti ad bestias tigres, a quibus insiliri, et nasci ex eodem fetu canes adeo acerrimos, 58 et fortes, ut in complexu leones prosternant.
passages.english: 28. Lycisci, as Pliny says, are dogs born from wolves and dogs when they happen to mix with each other. Indian women also are accustomed to have female dogs, tied up at night in the woods, admitted to tigers, by which they are mounted; and from the same litter dogs are born so very fierce and strong that they lay lions low in their grip.
passages.notes: 'Indæ feminæ' is evidently a corruption: the usual sense is 'the Indians [are accustomed to have] female dogs...'; translated so in effect but the reading is uncertain. Read 'canibus', 'alligatæ'; stray marks 'a', 'p', page number '58' omitted.

passages.original: Anguis vocabulum omnium serpentium genus, quod plicari et contorqueri potest. Et inde anguis, quod angulosus sit, et nunquam rectus. Angues autem apud gentiles n pro genils locorum erant habiti semper, unde et Persius: Pinge duos aogues, pueri, sacer est locus...
passages.english: Anguis (snake) is a word for the whole class of serpents, because it can be folded and twisted. And hence anguis, because it is angular (angulosus) and never straight. Among the pagans snakes were always held to be the genii of places; hence also Persius: 'Paint two snakes, boys: the place is sacred...'
passages.notes: Read 'geniis' and 'angues'; stray 'n' omitted.

passages.original: 10. d Vipera dicta, quod vi pariat. Nam cum venter ejus ad partum e ingemuerit, catuli non exspectantes naturæ maturam solutionem, corrosis ejus lateribus, vi erumpunt cum matris interitu. Lucanus: Viperei coeunt abrupto corpore nodi.
passages.english: 10. The viper (vipera) is so called because it gives birth by force (vi pariat). For when its belly groans toward birth, the young, not waiting for nature's timely release, gnaw through her sides and burst out by force, with the death of the mother. Lucan: 'The viper's coils join together from a torn-open body.'
passages.notes: Stray marks 'd', 'e' omitted.

passages.original: n Scytale serpens vocatus, eo quod tanta præfulget tergi varietate , ut notarum gratia aspicientes retardet, et quia reptando pigrior est, quos assequi non valet, miraculo sui stupentes capit. Tanti autem fervoris est, ut etiam hiemis tempore exuvias corporis ferventis exponat. De quo Lucanus : Et scytale sparsis etiam nunc sola pruinis Exuvias positura suas.
passages.english: The scytale serpent is so called because it gleams with such variety on its back that it delays onlookers by the charm of its markings; and because it is rather slow in crawling, it catches those it cannot overtake while they stand stunned in wonder at it. It is of such heat that even in wintertime it lays aside the slough of its burning body. Of it Lucan [says]: 'And the scytale, alone about to shed its skin while the frosts are still scattered.'
passages.notes: Stray 'n' omitted.

passages.original: Nam χέρσον dicunt Græci terram, ύδωρ aquam. Hic per quam labitur terram fumare facit, quem sic Macer describit : Seu terga expirant spumanlia virus; Seu terræ fumant, qua teter labilur aoguis. Et Lucanus: Tractique via fumante cbelydri.
passages.english: For the Greeks call earth chersos and water hydor. This [serpent] makes the ground smoke through which it glides; Macer describes it thus: 'Whether its foaming back breathes out poison, or the ground smokes where the foul snake glides.' And Lucan: 'And the chelydrus, whose trail smokes as it is drawn along.'
passages.notes: Read 'spumantia', 'labitur', 'anguis', 'chelydri'.

passages.original: 25. i Natrix, serpens aquam veneno inficiens. In quocunque enim fonte fuerit, eum veneno immiscet, de quo Lucanus : Et Natrix violator aquæ.
passages.english: 25. The natrix is a serpent that infects water with poison. For whatever spring it is in, it mixes poison into it; of it Lucan [says]: "And the natrix, violator of the water."
passages.notes: The stray "i" before Natrix is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: 26. I Cenchris, serpens inflexuosus, qui semper iter rectum efficit. De quo Lucanus : Et semper recto lapsurus limite cenchris. Semper enim directus ambulat. Nam si se torserit dum currit, statim crepat.
passages.english: 26. The cenchris is a serpent that does not bend, which always makes its way in a straight line. Of it Lucan [says]: "And the cenchris, always about to glide on a straight track." For it always moves straight ahead. For if it twists itself while it is moving, it immediately bursts.
passages.notes: The stray "I" before Cenchris is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: 27. h Parias, serpens, qui semper in cauda ambulat, et sulcum facere videtur. De quo idem Lucanus : Et contentus iter cauda sulcare parias.
passages.english: 27. The parias is a serpent that always moves on its tail and seems to make a furrow. Of it the same Lucan [says]: "And the parias, content to furrow its way with its tail."
passages.notes: The stray "h" is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: 29. j Jaculus serpens volans, de quo Lucanus : Jaculique volucres. Exsiliunt enim in arboribus, et dum aliquod animat obvium fuerit, 69 jactant se super illud, et perimunt; unde et jaculi dicti sunt. In Arabia autem serpentes sunt cum alis , quæ k sirenæ vocantur, quae plus currunt ab equis , sed ctiam et volare dicuntur, quorum tantum virus est, ut morsum ante mors insequatur quam dolor.
passages.english: 29. The jaculus is a flying serpent; of it Lucan [says]: "And the winged jaculi." For they leap up into trees, and when some animal comes in their way, they hurl themselves upon it and kill it; hence they are called jaculi ["javelins"]. In Arabia, moreover, there are serpents with wings, which are called sirens. They run faster than horses, and are also said to fly. Their venom is so powerful that death follows the bite before pain does.
passages.notes: Read "animal" for "animat" and "etiam" for "ctiam". The "69" is a page number and the stray "j" and "k" are footnote marks; all have been omitted. "plus currunt ab equis" is taken to mean "run faster than horses".

passages.original: 38. Stellio, de colore inditum nomen habet. Est enim tergore pictus lucentibus guttis in modum stellarum. De quo Ovidius : ..... aptumque colori Nomen habet, variis stellatus corpora guttis. a Hic autem scorpionibus adeo contrarius traditur, ut viso eo pavorem iis afferat, et torporem.
passages.english: 38. The stellio has its name from its colour. For its back is painted with shining spots like stars. Of it Ovid [says]: "...and it has a name suited to its colour, its body starred with various spots." It is said to be so hostile to scorpions that the sight of it brings them fear and numbness.
passages.notes: The stray "a" is a footnote mark and has been omitted. The ellipsis marks the edition's omission of the beginning of the quotation.

passages.original: 42. Unde non potest venenum nocere, nisi hominis tetigerit sanguinem. Lucanus : Noxia serpentum est admisto sanguine pestis. Omne autem venenum frigidum est, etideo anima, quæ ignea est, fugit venenum frigidum.ln naturalibus bonis, quae nobis et irrationabilibus animaniibus videmus esse communia, vivacitate quadam sensus serpens excellit.
passages.english: 42. Hence poison cannot do harm unless it touches a person's blood. Lucan [says]: "The serpents' plague is harmful once mixed with blood." All poison is cold, and so the soul, which is fiery, flees cold poison. Among the natural goods which we see to be common to us and to irrational animals, the serpent excels in a certain liveliness of sense.
passages.notes: The last sentence seems to begin a new section that has been run on without a break. Read "et ideo" and "In" for the scanning errors "etideo" and "ln", and "animantibus" for "animaniibus".

passages.original: 48. ) Pythagoras dicit de medulla hominis morlui, quæ in spina est, serpentem creari, quod eliam Ovidius in Metamorphosis libris commemorat, dicens : Sunt qui cum clauso putrefacta est spina sepulcro, Mutari credant. humanas augue medullas.
passages.english: 48. Pythagoras says that a serpent is generated from the marrow of a dead person, which is in the spine. Ovid also mentions this in the books of the Metamorphoses, saying: "There are those who believe that, when the spine has rotted in the closed tomb, human marrow is changed into a snake."
passages.notes: Read "mortui", "etiam" and "angue" for the scanning errors "morlui", "eliam" and "augue". The stray ")" has been omitted.

passages.original: 9. Eruca, frondium vermis, in oleribus, vel pampino involuta , ab erodendo dicta , de qua meminit d Plautus : Imitatus nequam bestiam et maleficam involutam in pampino. Implicat se eadem, e nec advolat, ut locusla, ut huc illucque discurrens, semipasta dimittat; sed permanet perituris frugibus, et tardo lapsu pigrisque morsibus universa consumit.
passages.english: 9. The eruca [caterpillar] is a worm of foliage, found on vegetables or wrapped in the vine-leaf; it is named from eating away (erodendo). Plautus mentions it: "Imitating the worthless and harmful beast wrapped in the vine-leaf." It wraps itself up, and does not fly off like the locust, which runs about here and there and leaves things half-eaten. Instead it stays on the crops that are doomed to perish, and with slow movement and sluggish bites it consumes everything.
passages.notes: The stray "d" and "e" are footnote marks and have been omitted. Read "locusta" for "locusla". In "ut huc illucque" the "ut" is taken to mean "which"; the syntax is loose.

passages.original: 45. Torpedo vocata, eo quod corpus torpescere faciat, si eam quisquam viventem tangat. i Narrat Plinius Secundus , « ex Indico mari torpedo etiam procul, et e longinquo, vel ii hasta virgaque at- tingatur, quamvis pravalidos lacertos torpescere, quamlibet ad cursum veloces pedes alligari. » Tanta enim vis ejus est, ut etiam aura corporis sui afficiat membra.
passages.english: 45. The torpedo [electric ray] is so called because it makes the body grow numb (torpescere) if anyone touches it while it is alive. Pliny the Second relates that "the torpedo from the Indian Sea, even when touched from afar and at a distance, with a spear or a rod, makes arms grow numb however strong they are, and binds feet however swift they are at running." For its power is so great that it affects the limbs even with the emanation of its body.
passages.notes: Read "vel" for "vel ii" (scanning error), "attingatur" for "at- tingatur", and "praevalidos" for "pravalidos". The stray "i" is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: 54. Pelorides, a Pelore promontorio Siciliae, ubi abundant, cognominatæ sunt. (Unde Virgilius dicit:) Ecce autem Boreas angusta ab sede Pelori.
passages.english: 54. The pelorides [a kind of shellfish] are named from Pelorus, a promontory of Sicily, where they are abundant. (Hence Virgil says:) "But look, Boreas [the north wind] from the narrow seat of Pelorus."

passages.original: 60. « Sfungia, a fingere, id est, nitidare et extergere dicta. Afranius : 86Accedo ad te, ut tibi cervicem fingam linteo, id est, extergam. Cicero : Effingebatur fungiis sanguis, id est, extergebatur. n Animat aulem esse docetur cruore inhærente petris. Unde, et dum abscinditur, sanguinem remittit.
passages.english: 60. The sponge (sfungia) is named from fingere, that is, to clean and wipe off. Afranius: "I come to you to 'fingere' your neck with a linen cloth," that is, to wipe it. Cicero: "The blood was wiped up (effingebatur) with sponges," that is, it was wiped off. It is shown to be animate by the blood clinging to rocks. Hence also, when it is cut off, it gives out blood.
passages.notes: 'aulem' read as 'autem'; '86' is a stray page/marginal mark.

passages.original: 63. q Animalium omnium in aquis viventium no. mina CXLIV, Plinius ait, divisa in generibus bellua-. rum, serpentium communium terrae, et aquae, cancrorum, concharum, locustarum, peloridum polypo- rum, solearum, lacertorum, et loliginum, et bis similla, ex quibus multa, quodam natura intellectu, temporum suorum ordinem agnoscunt, 87 quaedam vero in suis locis sine mutatione vagantur.
passages.english: 63. Pliny says that there are 144 names of all the animals living in the waters, divided into the kinds of sea-beasts, of serpents common to land and water, of crabs, shellfish, lobsters, giant mussels, octopuses, flatfish, lizard-fish, and squids, and things similar to these. Of these, many recognize the order of their seasons by a certain understanding given by nature, while some wander in their own places without change.
passages.notes: 'q' and '87' are footnote or page marks and are omitted. 'bis similla' is read as 'his similia'. 'quodam natura intellectu' is read as 'quodam naturae intellectu'. 'peloridum' (giant mussels) and 'lacertorum' (a kind of fish) are uncertain identifications.

passages.original: 14. Grues vero nomen de propria voce sumpseruni, tali enim sono susurrant. Hæ autem dum properant, unam sequuntur n ordine litterato. De quibus Lucanus : Et turbata perit dispersis littera pennis. Excelsa autem petunt, quo facilius videant quas petant terras.
passages.english: 14. Cranes (grues) took their name from their own call, for they make a murmuring sound of that kind. When they hurry along, they follow one [bird] in an order shaped like a letter. Of them Lucan [says]: 'And the letter is broken and lost as the wings scatter.' They make for high places so that they can more easily see the lands they are heading for.
passages.notes: 'sumpseruni' is read as 'sumpserunt' and 'n ordine' as 'in ordine'.

passages.original: 21. Ardea vocata, quasi ardua, id est, propter altos volatus. Lucanus : i Quodque ausa volare Ardea. j Formidat enim imbres, et super nubes evolat, ut procellas nubium sentire non possit; cum autern altius volaverit, significat tempestatem. Hanc multi k tantalum nominant.
passages.english: 21. The heron (ardea) is so called as if 'ardua' [lofty], that is, because of its high flights. Lucan: 'And the heron that has dared to fly.' For it fears rain, and flies up above the clouds so that it cannot feel the storms of the clouds; and when it has flown higher [than usual], it signals a storm. Many call it the tantalus.
passages.notes: The letters i, j, k are footnote marks and are omitted.

passages.original: 39. Bubo, a sono vocis compositum nomen liabct, avis feralis, onusta quidem plumis, sed gravi semper detenta pigritie; in sepulcris die noctuque versatur, et semper commorans in cavernis; de qua Ovidius : Foedaque fit volucris venturi nuntia luctus, Ignavus bubo dirum monialibus omen. Denique apud augures malum portendere fertur ; nam cum in urbe visa fuerit, solitudinem significari dicunt.
passages.english: 39. The eagle-owl (bubo) has a name formed from the sound of its call. It is a bird of death, loaded with feathers, but always held back by heavy sluggishness. It haunts tombs day and night and always lives in caves. Of it Ovid [says]: 'And it becomes a loathsome bird, messenger of coming grief, the sluggish owl, a dire omen for mortals.' Accordingly, among the augurs it is said to portend evil, for they say that when it has been seen in a city, it signifies desolation.
passages.notes: 'liabct' is read as 'habet'. 'monialibus' is read as 'mortalibus' (Ovid).

passages.original: 42. c Strix, nocturna avis habens nomen de sono vocis: quando enim clamat, stridet; de quo Lucanus : Quod trepidos bubo, quod Strix nocturna queruntur. 96 Haec avis vulgo amma dicitur, ab amando parvulos, unde, et lae praebere fertur nascentibus.
passages.english: 42. The screech-owl (strix) is a night bird that has its name from the sound of its call, for when it cries out it shrieks (stridet). Of it Lucan [says]: 'What the owl and the night screech-owl complain of to the fearful.' This bird is commonly called amma, from loving (amando) little ones, and so it is also said to offer milk to the newborn.
passages.notes: 'c' and '96' are marks and are omitted. 'lae' is read as 'lac' (milk).

passages.original: q Fucus est ntajor ape, crabrone minor. Dictus autem fucus, quod alienos labores edat, quasi fagus. Depascitur enim quod non laboravit; de quo Virgilius : Ignavum focos pecus a præsepibus arcent:
passages.english: The drone (fucus) is larger than a bee and smaller than a hornet. It is called fucus because it eats the labours of others, as if 'fagus' [eater]. For it feeds on what it did not work for. Of it Virgil [says]: 'They keep the drones, a lazy herd, away from the hives.'
passages.notes: The etymology plays on Greek phagein, 'to eat'. 'focos' is read as 'fucos'.

passages.original: 16. e Bibiones sunt qui in vino nascuntur, quos vulgo mustiones a musto appellant, node et Afranius : Ad me cum spectas, fabularique incipis, ex ore in oculos tuos bibiones involant.
passages.english: 16. Bibiones are those [insects] that are born in wine, which are commonly called mustiones from must; whence also Afranius: "When you look at me and begin to talk, bibiones fly from your mouth into your eyes."
passages.notes: 'node' read as 'unde'.

passages.original: 110 3. Interdum et cœlum pro aere accipitur, ubi venti et nubes, procellae et turbines fiunt. i Lucretius : Cœlo, qui dicitur aer. Et psalmus volucres cœli appellat, cum manifestum sit aves in aere volare; j et nos in consuetudine hunc aerem coelum appellamus; nam cum de sereno vel nubilo quaerimus, aliquando dicimus : Qualis est aer?
passages.english: 3. Sometimes 'sky' (caelum) is also taken for the air, where winds and clouds, storms and whirlwinds occur. Lucretius: 'In the sky, which is called air.' And the Psalm speaks of 'birds of the sky', though it is plain that birds fly in the air. And we too, in common usage, call this air 'sky'; for when we ask about fair or cloudy weather, we sometimes say: 'What is the air like?'
passages.notes: '110' and the letters i, j are marks and are omitted.

passages.original: 1. Aer est inanitas plurimum habens admistum raritatis, # quam caetera elementa. De quo Virgilius : c Longum per inane secutus. Aer dictus ἀπὸ τοῡ αἲρειν, ab eo quod ferat terram, vel ab eo quod feratur. Hic autem partim ad coelestem, partirn ad terrenam materiam pertinet ; nam ille subtilis, ubi ventosi ac procellosi motus non possunt existere, ad cælestem pertinet partem;
passages.english: 1. Air is an emptiness that has much more thinness mixed in [it] than the other elements. Of it Virgil [says]: 'Following through the long void.' Air is named apo tou airein [from lifting], either because it carries the earth or because it is carried. It belongs partly to heavenly and partly to earthly matter. For that fine air, where windy and stormy motions cannot arise, belongs to the heavenly part;
passages.notes: '#' likely stands for a lost 'magis' or 'plus', giving 'more than'. 'c' is a mark and is omitted.

passages.original: 4. Imbres autem, et ad nubes, et ad pluviis pertinent, k dicti a Græco vocabulo, quod terram in- ebrient ad germinandum. Ex his enim cuncta creantur, 1 unde, et Lucretius : Ex igni terra, atque anima nascuntur et imbri. Est autem nomen Graecum.
passages.english: 4. Rain-showers (imbres) belong both to clouds and to rains. They are named from a Greek word, because they drench (inebrient) the earth so that it sprouts. For from these all things are created; hence Lucretius also [says]: 'From fire, earth, air and rain are [things] born.' And it is a Greek name.
passages.notes: The letters k and 1 are marks and are omitted. The Greek source word is uncertain, probably ombros. 'pluviis' is read as 'pluvias'.

passages.original: 5. Vulturnus, quod alle tonat; de quo Lucretius: Altitonans Vulturnus, et Auster fulmine pollens.
passages.english: 5. Vulturnus [is so called] because it thunders on high; of it Lucretius [says]: 'High-thundering Vulturnus, and Auster mighty with lightning.'
passages.notes: 'alle' is read as 'alte'. Vulturnus and Auster are winds.

passages.original: 17. Aura ab aere dicta, quasi aerea, quod lenis sit motus aeris. Agitatus enim aer auram facit, unde et k Lucretius: Aereas auras.
passages.english: 17. A breeze (aura) is named from air (aer), as if 'airy' (aerea), because it is a gentle motion of the air. For air when stirred makes a breeze, which is why Lucretius also [says]: 'airy breezes'.
passages.notes: The stray 'k' before 'Lucretius' is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: 2. Fretum autem appellatum, quod ibi semper mare ferveat ; nam fretum est aNgustum, et quasi fervens mare, ab undarum fervore nominatum, ut Gaditanum, vel Siculum; nam freta dicta Varro ait, quasi fervida, id est, fervenlia, et motum fervoris habentia.
passages.english: 2. A strait (fretum) is so called because the sea is always seething (fervere) there; for a strait is a narrow and, as it were, seething sea, named from the seething of the waves, like the [strait] of Gades or the Sicilian; for Varro says that straits (freta) are so called as if fervida, that is, fervent, and having the motion of seething.
passages.notes: 'fervenlia' read as 'ferventia'.

passages.original: Syrtes autem i SaJlustius a tractu vocari dicit, quod omnia ad se trahant, g et appropinquanti vadoso mari hæreant. Hæ autem ad mare Ægyptium vicinae Bunt, et pariter admiscentur. h Vado vero sunt, per quae in mari, vel in fluminibus homines, vel animalia pedibus vadunt ; quae Virgilius brevia appellat, Græci βραχεῑα.
passages.english: Sallust says that the Syrtes are named from 'dragging' (tractus), because they drag everything to themselves and stick fast to anything that approaches the shallow sea. These lie near the Egyptian sea and are mingled with it. Fords (vada), on the other hand, are [the places] through which people or animals go (vadunt) on foot in the sea or in rivers; Virgil calls these 'shallows' (brevia), the Greeks brakheia.
passages.notes: Footnote marks (i, g, h) omitted. 'SaJlustius' read as Sallustius and 'Bunt' as sunt. The etymology plays on Greek syrein, 'to drag'.

passages.original: 5. Unda vero, eminens liquor, qui semper in motu est. Lucretius : d Aerias undas , id est, motus , et corpus illud quod refluctuat. Nam nec unda per se aqua est, sed aqua in motu quodam et agitatione, quasi ab eundo, et redeundo unda vocata.
passages.english: 5. A wave (unda) is water that rises up and is always in motion. Lucretius [writes]: 'airy waves', that is, motions, and that body which surges back and forth. For a wave is not water in itself, but water in a certain motion and agitation; it is called unda as if from going and returning (eundo, redeundo).
passages.notes: Footnote mark 'd' omitted.

passages.original: Fluvius est perennis aquarum decursus, a fluen- do perpetim dictus. Proprie autem flumen ipsa aqua, fluvius cursus aquæ. Prius autem flumen quam fluvias, id est, prior aqua quam decursus. Duo sunt fluminum genera : unum torrens, alterum vivum, de quo Virgilius : Donec me flumine vivo, abluero.
passages.english: A river (fluvius) is a perennial running of waters, named from flowing (fluendo) continually. Properly, however, flumen is the water itself, fluvius the course of the water. Flumen comes before fluvius, that is, the water before the running. There are two kinds of rivers: one a torrent, the other living, of which Virgil [says]: 'Until I have washed myself in a living stream.'
passages.notes: 'fluvias' read as fluvius. 'Living' water means perennial, spring-fed water.

passages.original: 2. h Torrens est aqua veniens cum impetu. Dictus autem torrens, 133 quia pluvia crescit, siccitate torrescit id est, arescit. i De quo Pacuvius : Flammeo vapore torrens terræ fetum exusserit. Cui Graeci ab biemeuomen dederunt, nos ab æstate; illi a tempore quo succressit , nos a lempore quo siccatur.
passages.english: 2. A torrent is water that comes with violent force. It is called a torrent because it swells with rain and is parched (torrescit), that is, dries up, in drought. Of this Pacuvius [says]: "Scorching (torrens) with fiery heat, it would have burned up the offspring of the earth." The Greeks gave it [its name] from winter, we from summer; they from the season in which it swells, we from the season in which it dries up.
passages.notes: 'ab biemeuomen' is garbled; presumably a Greek word from 'cheimōn' (winter), i.e. 'cheimarrhous' or similar. Pacuvius line obscure; translated literally. Stray letters 'h', 'i' and page number '133' omitted.

passages.original: Euphrates fluvius Mesopotamiæ, de paradiso exoriens, copiosissimus gemmis , qui per mediaM Babyloniam influit; hic a frugibus , vel ab ubertate nomen accepit. c Nam Uebraice EPHRATA fertilitas interpretatur; Mesopotamiam enim in quibusdam locis ita irrigat, sicut Nilus Alexandriam. a Sallustius au- tem auctor certissimus asserit Tigrim et Euphratem uno fonte manare in Armenia, qui per diversa euntes longius dividuntur , spatio medio relicto multorum millium , quæ tamen terra, quae ab ipsis ambitur, Mesopotamia dicitur. Ex quo Hieronymus animadvertit aliter de paradisi fluminibus intelligendum.
passages.english: The Euphrates is a river of Mesopotamia. It rises from paradise, is very rich in gems, and flows through the middle of Babylonia. It took its name from crops (fruges) or from fertility, for in Hebrew EPHRATA is interpreted 'fertility'; and indeed in some places it irrigates Mesopotamia just as the Nile does Alexandria. Sallust, a most reliable authority, states that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from a single spring in Armenia. Going in different directions, they become widely separated, leaving a space of many miles between them; the land enclosed by them is called Mesopotamia. From this Jerome observed that the rivers of paradise must be understood in another way.
passages.notes: Footnote marks (c, a) omitted; 'Uebraice' read as Hebraice.

passages.original: 12. Hydaspes fuit Medorum rex antiquissimus, ex quo amnis Orientis nomen accepit, qui nunc Hydaapes dicitur, de quo Lucanus : Vastis lndus aquis mistum non senlit Hydaspen. Et, qua Medus Hydaspes 136 Accedit Pelago, Phœbi surgentis ab igne. e Qui dum sit fluvius Persarum, dicitur tamen contra Orientem decurrere.
passages.english: 12. Hydaspes was a very ancient king of the Medes, from whom a river of the East took its name, which is now called the Hydaspes. Of it Lucan [says]: 'The Indus with its vast waters does not feel the Hydaspes mingled with it.' And: 'where the Median Hydaspes reaches the sea, by the fire of the rising sun.' Although it is a river of the Persians, it is nevertheless said to run down toward the East.
passages.notes: Footnote mark 'e' and page number '136' omitted; 'Hydaapes' read as Hydaspes. The second quotation appears to be a conflation of separate lines.

passages.original: 13. f Araris duvius Germaniæ. De quo Virgilius : Aut Ararim Parthus hibet, aut Germania Tigrim.
passages.english: 13. The Arar is a river of Germany. Of it Virgil [says]: 'Either the Parthian will drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris.'
passages.notes: 'duvius' read as fluvius and 'hibet' as bibet. The Arar (Saône) is in fact a Gallic river.

passages.original: Pactolus fluvius Asiæ , arenas aereas trahens. De quo Virgilius : Pactolusque irrigat auro : quem pro aurato fluore alii Chrysorhoam vocant.
passages.english: The Pactolus is a river of Asia that carries bronze-coloured sands. Of it Virgil [says]: 'and the Pactolus waters [the fields] with gold'. Because of its golden flow others call it the Chrysorrhoas ('gold-flowing').
passages.notes: 'aereas' (bronze) may be an error for 'aureas' (golden), which the context suggests.

passages.original: Mæander amnis Asiæflexuosus, qui, recurrentibus ripis 138 inter Canam et loniam, praecipitatur in sinum qui Miletum dividit et Prienen. Mæander autem vocatus, quod sit flexuosus et nunquam currat rectus. De quo Ovidius : Quique recurvatus ludit Mæander m undis.
passages.english: The Meander is a winding river of Asia. With banks that turn back on themselves, it runs between Caria and Ionia and rushes down into the gulf that divides Miletus and Priene. It is called Meander because it is winding and never runs straight. Of it Ovid [says]: 'and the Meander, which, bending back, plays in its waves.'
passages.notes: 'Canam' read as Cariam and 'loniam' as Ioniam. Page number '138' and footnote mark 'm' omitted.

passages.original: 34. Bætis fluvius, qui et Bæticæ provinciae nomen dedit, de quo Martialis : 140 Bætis olivifera crioem redimfle corona Aurea, qui nitidis vellera lingis aquis m eo quod ibi lanæ pulchro colore tinguntur. Bætis. autem dictus, eo quod humili solo decurrat. βαθύ n enim Græci humile, vel mersum vocant.
passages.english: 34. The Baetis is a river that also gave its name to the province of Baetica. Of it Martial [says]: 'Baetis, your hair bound with an olive-bearing crown, who dye golden fleeces in your bright waters', because there wool is dyed a beautiful colour. It is called Baetis because it runs down through low-lying ground; for the Greeks call what is low or sunken bathy.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors were corrected: 'crioem redimfle' read as crinem redimite, and 'lingis' as tingis. Page number '140' and marks 'm', 'n' omitted.

passages.original: d Proprie autem terra, ad distinctionem aquae, arida nuncupatur, sicut 142 Scriptura ait quod vocaverit Deus terram aridam. Naturalis enim proprietas siccitas est terrae; nam ut humida sit, boc aquarum affinitate sortitur. e Cujus motum alii dicunt ventum esse in concavis ejus, qui motus eam movet. Sallustius : Venti per cava terræ præcipitati rupli aliquot montes tumulique sedere.
passages.english: Properly, however, earth, to distinguish it from water, is called 'dry land', as Scripture says that God called the earth dry land. For dryness is the natural property of earth; that it is moist, it gets from its affinity with the waters. Some say that its motion is wind in its hollows, and that this motion moves it. Sallust: 'Winds rushing down through the hollows of the earth, several mountains and hills burst open and sank.'
passages.notes: Stray letters (d, e) are footnote marks, omitted, as is the page number 142. 'boc' read as 'hoc'. 'rupli' read as 'rupti'.

passages.original: 3. Alii aquam dicunt genitalem in terris moveri, et f eas simul concutere, sicut vas, ut dicit Lucretius. Alii σϕγγοειδη̃ terram volunt, cujus plerumque latentes ruinæ superposita cuncta concutiunt. s Terrae quoque hiatus, aut motu aquae inferioris fit, aut crebris tonitruis, aut de concavis terræerumpentibus ventis.
passages.english: Others say that generative water moves in the earth and shakes the lands together with it, as [water shakes] a vessel, as Lucretius says. Others hold that the earth is sponge-like, and that its hidden collapses, for the most part, shake everything set above them. A gaping of the earth, too, is caused either by the motion of the water below, or by frequent thunder, or by winds bursting out of the hollows of the earth.
passages.notes: The Greek σπογγοειδῆ ('sponge-like') is garbled in the scan. 'eas' (feminine plural) is taken to refer to 'terris'. Footnote marks (f, s) omitted.

passages.original: 41. 8 Phrygia dicta a Phrygia Æsopi filia. t Hæc Dardania a Dardano Jovis filio dicta. De u quo Homerus ait: Quem primum genuit cælesti Jupiter arce. v Hic enim profectus de Corito civitate primus venit in Phrygiam. Est autem regio x Troadi superjecta ab Aquilonis parte Galatiæ, a Meridiana vicina est Lycaoniæ, ab Oriente Lydiæ adhæret, ab Occidentc Hellesponto mari terminatur.
passages.english: Phrygia is named after Phrygia, the daughter of Aesop. It is [also called] Dardania, after Dardanus, the son of Jupiter. Of him Homer says: 'Whom Jupiter begot first from the heavenly citadel.' For he set out from the city of Corythus and was the first to come into Phrygia. It is a region lying above the Troad. On the north it [borders] Galatia, on the south it is neighbour to Lycaonia, on the east it adjoins Lydia, and on the west it is bounded by the sea of the Hellespont.
passages.notes: Numbering and footnote marks omitted. 'Corito' is taken as Corythus. The sentence about the north is elliptical in the Latin. 'Aesop' as Phrygia's father is as the text has it.

passages.original: Unde nomen urbis illius, vel potius insulæ fuit. u Nam Tenes iste infamatus, quod cum noverca sua concubuisset, fugiens hanc insulam vacuam cultoribus obtinuit; unde et Tenedos insula dicta est; a sic Cicero :Tenen ipsum, cujus ex nomine Tenedos, nominatur.
passages.english: Hence came the name of that city, or rather of the island. For this Tenes was disgraced because he had [allegedly] slept with his stepmother. Fleeing, he took possession of this island, which was empty of inhabitants, and so the island was called Tenedos. So Cicero [says]: 'Tenes himself, from whose name Tenedos is named.'
passages.notes: Footnote marks omitted. The bracketed 'allegedly' reflects 'infamatus' ('defamed').

passages.original: Hisioria dicit ex Jasone natum fuisse Philomelum et Plutum ; ex Philomelo Parcantum genitum, qui de suo nomine Paron insulam et oppidum appellavit, prius autem Minoia, deinde Paros dicta. i De qua Virgilius : Niveamqque Paron. Gignit enim marmor candidissimum, quod Parium dicunt. MiNUit et sardan lapidem, marmoribus cuidem præstantiorem, sed inter gemmas vilissimum.
passages.english: History says that Philomelus and Plutus were born of Jason, and that from Philomelus was begotten Paros, who named the island and town Paros after his own name. It was first called Minoia, then Paros. Of it Virgil [says]: 'and snowy Paros'. For it produces a very white marble, which they call Parian. It also produces the sard stone, superior indeed to marbles, but the cheapest among gems.
passages.notes: 'Parcantum' is corrupt; the sense requires the eponym Paros. 'MiNUit' read as 'gignit' and 'cuidem' as 'quidem'. 'Hisioria' read as 'Historia'.

passages.original: 35. Tapsus insula stadiis decem a Siciliaremota jacens, et planior, unde et nuncupata. De qua Virgilius : a Tapsumque jacentem.
passages.english: Thapsus is an island lying ten stadia from Sicily, and rather flat, from which it is also named. Of it Virgil [says]: 'and low-lying Thapsus'.
passages.notes: The etymology plays on 'iacens' ('lying low').

passages.original: 36. Æoliæ insulæ Siciliæ appellatæ ab r Æolo Hippotæ filio, quem poetæ finxeront regem fuisse ventorum, sed, ut Varro dicit, rector fuit istarum insularum, et quia ex earum nebulis et fumo futuros prædicebat flatusventorum, ab imperitis visus est ventos sua potestate retinuisse. Eædem insulae et Vulcaniæ vocantur, quodet ipsae,;sicut Ætna ardeant.
passages.english: 36. The Aeolian islands of Sicily are named from Aeolus son of Hippotes, whom the poets fabled to have been king of the winds; but, as Varro says, he was ruler of these islands, and because from their mists and smoke he foretold the coming blasts of the winds, he seemed to the ignorant to have held the winds in his own power. These same islands are also called Vulcanian, because they too, like Etna, burn.

passages.original: 42. Haec autem insula Græce ϰὺρνη dicitur, a Gyrno Herculis filio habitata. De qua Virgilius : Cyrnœas taxos. I Dividitur autem a Sardinia xx mil- lium freto, cincta Ligustici aequoris sinu ad prospectum Italiæ. Est autem multis promontoriis angu- losa, gignens laetissima pabula, et lapidem quem cathochiten Graeci vocant.
passages.english: This island is called in Greek Kyrnē, having been inhabited by Cyrnus, son of Hercules. Of it Virgil [says]: 'Cyrnean yews'. It is separated from Sardinia by a strait of twenty miles, and is surrounded by a gulf of the Ligurian sea, facing Italy. It is angular with many promontories, producing very rich pasture and a stone which the Greeks call *catochites*.
passages.notes: The island is Corsica, named in the preceding text. 'Gyrno' read as Cyrnus.

passages.original: vulgus majoricam et minoricam nuncupant. 182 In iis primum insulis inventa est funda, qua lapides emit. tuntur, unde et Baleares dictae: i βάλλειν enim Graece mittere dicitur; k unde et ballista, quasi missa et fundibalum. Virgilius : Balearis verbere fundas.
passages.english: the common people call [them] Majorica and Minorica. In these islands the sling, with which stones are hurled, was first invented, and so they were called the Baleares: for in Greek 'to throw' is *ballein*. Hence also *ballista*, as if 'thrown', and *fundibalum* [a sling-engine]. Virgil: 'the lashes of the Balearic sling'.
passages.notes: 'emit. tuntur' read as 'emittuntur'. The passage begins mid-sentence.

passages.original: 183 4. 0 Pelorum promontorium Siciliæ respiciens ad Aquilonem, secundum Sallustium dictum a gubernatore Annibalis illic sepulto.
passages.english: Pelorus is a promontory of Sicily facing north, named, according to Sallust, after Hannibal's helmsman, who was buried there.

passages.original: 9. Olympus mons Macedoniae nimium præcelsus, ita ut sub illo nubes esse dicantur (h De quo Virgilius : Nubes excessit Olympus). Dictus autem i Olympus quasi Ololampus ( id est, i quasi cœlum). Hic mons Macedoniam dividit a Thracia.
passages.english: Olympus is a mountain of Macedonia, exceedingly lofty, so that the clouds are said to be below it (of which Virgil [says]: 'Olympus rose above the clouds'). It is called Olympus as if 'Ololampus', that is, as if 'heaven'. This mountain divides Macedonia from Thrace.
passages.notes: The etymology ('wholly shining') is Isidore's own.

passages.original: Item Ceraunii sunt montes Epiri, a crebris dicti fulminibus. Graece enim fulmen ϰέραυνος dicitur. 13. Apenninus mons appellatus, quasi Alpes Pœninœ,quia Hannibal veniens ad ltaliam easdem Alpes aperuit, unde et Virgilius : Alpes immittet apertas. Has enim Hannibal m post bella Hispaniæ aceto rupit. Juvenalis : Et montem rupit aceto. Et inde loca ipsa quae rupit Pœninœ Alpes vocantur.
passages.english: Likewise the Ceraunian mountains are mountains of Epirus, named from their frequent thunderbolts, for in Greek a thunderbolt is called *keraunos*. 13. The Apennine mountain was so called as if [from] the Pennine Alps, because Hannibal, coming into Italy, opened up these Alps; hence also Virgil: "He will send in the opened Alps." For after the wars in Spain Hannibal broke through these with vinegar. Juvenal: "And he broke the mountain with vinegar." And from this the very places that he broke through are called the Pennine Alps.
passages.notes: The stray 'm' after 'Hannibal' is taken as a footnote mark and omitted. 'Pœninœ' is read as 'Poeninae'.

passages.original: 17. Calpe mons in ultimis finibus Oceani, qui diri. mit Europam ab Africa , quem Atlantis finem esse dicunt. p De quo Lucanus : Hesperiam Calpen, summumque implevit Atlantem. Atlas Promethei 187 frater fuit, et rex Africae, a quo astrologiæ artem prius dicunt excogitatam, ideoque dictus est sustinuisse coelum. Ob eruditionem igitur ejus disciplinæ et scientiam coeli, nomen ejus in montem Africae derivatum est, qui nunc Atlas cognomi- natur, qui propter altitudinem suam, quasi coeli ma- cbinam atque astra sustentare videmur.
passages.english: 17. Calpe is a mountain at the farthest bounds of the Ocean, which divides Europe from Africa, and which they say is the end of Atlas. Of it Lucan [says]: "He filled western Calpe and highest Atlas." Atlas was the brother of Prometheus and king of Africa, by whom, they say, the art of astrology was first devised, and for that reason he is said to have held up the sky. So because of his learning in that discipline and his knowledge of the sky, his name was transferred to a mountain of Africa, which is now called Atlas, and which, because of its height, seems as it were to hold up the structure of the sky and the stars.
passages.notes: 'diri. mit' is read as 'dirimit'. 'videmur' ("we seem") is read as 'videtur' ("it seems"). The stray 'p' and the number '187' are taken as footnote and page marks and omitted.

passages.original: 18. Alpes autem proprie montes Galliæ sunt, de quibus Virgilius : Aerias Alpes. Et dicendo aerlas; verbum expressit a verbo. Nam a Gallorom lingua Alpes montes alti vocantur. Hae sunt enim qoae Italiæ murorum exhibent vicem.
passages.english: 18. The Alps, properly, are the mountains of Gaul, of which Virgil [says]: The airy Alps. And in saying 'airy' he rendered word for word. For in the language of the Gauls high mountains are called Alps. These are what serve Italy in place of walls.
passages.notes: 'verbum expressit a verbo' is obscure: perhaps that 'airy' reproduces the sense of the Gaulish word ('high').

passages.original: 24. d Solum est omne, quod sustinet, a Soliditate dicium scilicet, unde et de mari Virgilius ait: Subtrahiturque solum.
passages.english: 24. Ground (*solum*) is everything that supports [something], named, that is, from solidity (*soliditas*); hence Virgil also says of the sea: "And the ground is drawn away from under [them]."

passages.original: 35. k Amœna locI Verrius Flaccus dicta ait, eo quod solum amorem præstent, et ad se amanda alliciant. Varro, quod sine munere sunt, nec quidquam in his officii, quasi amunia, hoc est, sine fructu, unde et nullus fructus exsolvitur. inde etiam nihil præstantes immunes vocamur.
passages.english: 35. Verrius Flaccus says pleasant places (amoena) are so called because they offer only love (amor) and entice [people] to love them. Varro [says it is] because they are without duty (munus), and there is no service in them, as if amunia, that is, without yield, whence also no produce is rendered. Hence also we who render nothing are called immune (immunes).

passages.original: 37. n Æstiva sunt loci umbrosa, iii quibus per æstatem vitant pecora solis ardorem. Statius : Et umbrosi pituere aestiva Lycæi. f
passages.english: 37. Summer pastures (*aestiva*) are shady places in which flocks avoid the heat of the sun during the summer. Statius: "And the summer pastures of shady Lycaeus grew foul."
passages.notes: 'iii' is read as 'in'. 'pituere' is unclear: it may stand for 'putuere' ("grew foul") or 'patuere' ("lay open").

passages.original: De a auctoribus condilarum urbium plerumque dissensio invenitur, adeo ut ne urbis quidem Romæ origo possit diligenter agnosci. Nam Salluslius dicit : Urbem Romam, sicuti ego accepi, condidere, acque habuere initio Trojani, et cum iis Aborigines. Alii dicunt ab Evandro, secundum quod Virgilius : Tunc rex Kvandrus Romanae conditor arcis. Alii A Romulo, ut : En hujus, nate, auspiciis illa inclyta Roma
passages.english: Disagreement is very often found about the founders of cities, so much so that not even the origin of the city of Rome can be known with certainty. For Sallust says: "The city of Rome, as I have learned, was founded and at first held by the Trojans, and with them the Aborigines." Others say [it was founded] by Evander, according to which Virgil [says]: "Then King Evander, founder of the Roman citadel." Others [say] by Romulus, as [in]: "Behold, son, under his auspices that glorious Rome
passages.notes: 'acque' is read as 'atque' and 'Kvandrus' as 'Evandrus'. The passage breaks off in the middle of the quotation.

passages.original: b Cum Cyrus maritimas urbes Græciæ occuparet, et Phocenses ab eo expugnati omnibus angustiis premerentur, juraverunt, ut profugerent quam longissime ab imperio Persarum, ubi ne nomen quidem eorum audirent, c atqueila in ultimos Galliae sinus navibus profecti, armisque se adversus Gallicam feritatem tuentes, Massiliam condiderunt, et ex nomine ducis nuncupaverunt. Hos a Varro trilingues esse ait, quod et Graece loquantur, et Latine, et Gallice.
passages.english: When Cyrus was seizing the coastal cities of Greece, and the Phocaeans, conquered by him, were pressed by every hardship, they swore to flee as far as possible from the dominion of the Persians, where they would not even hear their name; and so, setting out by ships into the furthest bays of Gaul, and defending themselves with arms against Gallic savagery, they founded Massilia and named it after the name of their leader. Varro says that these people are trilingual, because they speak Greek, Latin and Gaulish.
passages.notes: 'atqueila' read as 'atque ita'. The claim that Massilia was named from its leader's name is as in the text.

passages.original: Urbs vocata ab orbe, quod antiquitus civitates in orbem fiebant, 0 vel ab urbo parte aratri, quo muri designabantur, unde 209 est illud p: Optavitque locum regno, et concludere sulco. Locus enim futurae civitatis sulco designabatur, id est, aratro. q Cato : Qui urbem , inquit, novam condet, tauro et vacca aret, ubi araverit, murum faciat, ubi portam vult este, aratrum sustollat, et portet, et portam vocet.
passages.english: A city (*urbs*) is named from a circle (*orbis*), because in ancient times cities were made in a circle; or from *urbus*, a part of the plough with which the walls were marked out. Hence that [line]: "And he chose a place for his kingdom, and to enclose [it] with a furrow." For the site of a future city was marked out with a furrow, that is, with a plough. Cato says: "Whoever founds a new city should plough with a bull and a cow. Where he has ploughed, let him make the wall; where he wants there to be a gate, let him lift the plough and carry it, and call [that place] a gate."
passages.notes: The stray marks '0', 'p', 'q' and '209' are omitted. 'urbo' is read as 'urbus', the plough-beam. 'este' is read as 'esse'.

passages.original: 4. Ideo autem urbs aratro circumdabatur dispari sexu juvencorum propter commistionem familiarum, et imaginem serentis, fructumque reddentis. a Urhs autem aratro conditur, aratro evertitur. Unde Horatius : Imprimeretque muris hostile aratrum.
passages.english: 4. And the reason a city was encircled by a plough drawn by young cattle of different sex was the joining of families, and the image of one who sows and yields fruit. A city, moreover, is founded by the plough and overthrown by the plough. Hence Horace: "And [that] the enemy plough should be pressed upon the walls."
passages.notes: 'Urhs' is read as 'Urbs'.

passages.original: 2. Omne aedificium antiqui ædem appellaverunt. Alii ædem ab edendo quidem sumpsisse nomen existimant, dantes exempfum de Plauto : Si vocassem vos in ædem ad prandium
passages.english: 2. The ancients called every building an *aedes*. Some, indeed, think that *aedes* took its name from eating (*edendo*), giving an example from Plautus: "If I had called you into the house for lunch
passages.notes: The passage breaks off in the middle of the quotation.

passages.original: 4. Armarium locus est ubi quarumcunque artium instrumenta ponuntur. Armamentarium vero ubi tantum tela armorum. Unde Juvenalis : Quidquid habent telorum armamentaria cœli. Dicta autem utraque ab armis, id est, brachiis quibus exercentur.
passages.english: 4. An *armarium* (cupboard) is a place where the tools of any crafts are kept, but an *armamentarium* (arsenal) [is a place] where only weapons are kept. Hence Juvenal: "Whatever weapons the arsenals of heaven hold." Both are named from *armi*, that is, the arms with which [the tools and weapons] are used.

passages.original: Pistrinum, quasi pilistrinum, quia pilo antea tundebant granum. i Unde et apud veteres non molitores, sed pistores dicti sunt, quasi pinsores, k a pinsendis granis frumenti, molae enim nondum usus erat, sed granum pilo pinsebant. Unde Virgilius : Nunc torrete igni fruges, nunc frangite saxo
passages.english: A mill (*pistrinum*) [is so called] as if *pilistrinum*, because formerly they pounded grain with a pestle (*pilum*). Hence among the ancients [millers] were called not *molitores* but *pistores*, as if *pinsores*, from pounding (*pinsere*) the grains of wheat; for the use of the millstone did not yet exist, and they pounded the grain with a pestle. Hence Virgil: "Now parch the grain with fire, now break it with stone
passages.notes: The stray marks 'i' and 'k' are omitted. The passage breaks off in the middle of the quotation.

passages.original: Prima species fori locus est in civitate ad exercendas nundinas relictus; secunda, ubi magistratus Ju dicare solet; tertia, quam supra diximus, quam calcatorium I. nominamus; quarta, spatia plana in navibus. De quibus Virgilius: Laxatquefdros. Lacus dictus, quia ibi decurrit frUgum liquor.
passages.english: The first kind of *forum* is a place in a city set aside for holding markets; the second, where a magistrate is accustomed to give judgement; the third, the one we spoke of above, which we call the treading-floor; the fourth, the flat spaces in ships. Of these Virgil [says]: "And he loosens the decks (*foros*)." The vat (*lacus*) is so called because the liquid of the fruits runs down there.
passages.notes: "Laxatquefdros" is a scanning error for "laxatque foros". "Ju dicare" is read as "iudicare" and "frUgum" as "frugum". The stray "I." before "nominamus" is taken as a footnote mark and omitted.

passages.original: 4. i Janua a Jano quodam appellatur, cui gentiles omnem introitum, vel exitum sacraverunt. Unde g Lucanus: Ferrea belligeri compescat limina Jani. Eat autem primus domus ingressus, h caetera intra januam ostia vocantur generaliter. i Ostium est, per quod ab aliquo arcemur ingressu, ab obstando dictum, sive ostium, quia ostendit aliquid intus.
passages.english: The door (*ianua*) is named from a certain Janus, to whom the pagans consecrated every entrance or exit. Hence Lucan: "Let him close the iron threshold of warlike Janus." It is the first entrance of a house; the other [doors] inside the main door are generally called *ostia*. An *ostium* is that by which we are kept from entering somewhere, named from 'obstructing' (*obstando*); or else *ostium* because it shows (*ostendit*) something inside.
passages.notes: "Eat" is read as "Est". The stray letters g, h and i are footnote marks and are omitted.

passages.original: 6. b Laquearia sunt, quæ cameram subtegunt, et ornant. quæ et lacuniara dicantur. a Principaliter autem lacus dicitur, ut Lucilius : resultant ædesque, tacusque. Cujus diminutio lacMnar facit, ut Horatius : ..... Neque aureum Mea renidet in domo lacunar. Inde fit alia diminutio lacunarium, et per ὰντὶστιχον laquearium.
passages.english: 6. Laquearia (panelled ceilings) are what cover and adorn the vault beneath; they are also called lacunaria. But primarily it is called lacus, as Lucilius [says]: "the house and the panelled ceiling resound." Its diminutive makes lacunar, as Horace [says]: "Nor does a golden panelled ceiling gleam in my house." From this comes another diminutive, lacunarium, and by antistoichon (letter substitution) laquearium.
passages.notes: 'tacusque' read as 'lacusque'; 'lacMnar' as 'lacunar'.

passages.original: 6. e Omnis autem ager, ut Varro docet, quadrifariam dividitur. Aut enim arvus est ager, id est, saLionalis; aut consitus, id est , aptus arboribus ; aut pascuus, qui herbis tantum et animalibus vacat; aut floreus, in quo sunt horti apibus congruentes et floribus.
passages.english: 6. Every field, as Varro teaches, is divided in four ways. For a field is either arable, that is, for sowing; or planted, that is, suited to trees; or pasture, which is given over only to grasses and animals; or flowering, in which there are gardens suited to bees and flowers.
passages.notes: 'saLionalis' read as 'sationalis'.

passages.original: 8. f Seges ager est in quo seritur, unde et Virgilius: Illa seges demum votis respondet avari Agricolae.
passages.english: A crop-field (*seges*) is a field in which [seed] is sown (*seritur*); hence Virgil too: "That crop-field at last answers the prayers of the greedy farmer."

passages.original: 6. Strata dicta, quasi vulgi pedibus trita. Lucretius : Strataque jam vulgi pedibus detrita viarum. Ipsa est et delapidala, id est, lapidibus strata. Primi Mutem Pœni dicuntur lapidibus vias stravisse, 243 postea Romani eas per omnem pene orbem disposuerunt propter rectitudinem itinerum, et ne plebs esset otiosa.
passages.english: A paved road (*strata*) is so called as if worn (*trita*) by the feet of the common people. Lucretius: "And the paved ways of the roads now worn down by the feet of the common people." It is also [called] *delapidata*, that is, paved with stones. The Carthaginians are said to have been the first to pave roads with stones; afterwards the Romans laid them out through almost the whole world, for the straightness of journeys and so that the common people should not be idle.
passages.notes: "delapidala" is read as "delapidata", and "Mutem" as "autem".

passages.original: Eit autem colore ferrugineus, Med probatur cum ferro adjunctus ejus fecerit raptum. 0 Nam adeo apprehendit ferrum, ut catenam faciat annulorum. Unde et eum vulgus ferrum vivum appellat.— i. Liquorem quoque titri, ut ferrum, trahere creditnE, cujus tanta vis est (p ut refert beatissiimus Augustinus) quod quidam eumdem magnetem lapidem tenuerit sub vase argenteo, ferrumque super argentum posuerit, deinde subtermovente manu eum lapide ferrum cursim desuper movebatur. q Unde factum est, ut in quodam 254 templo simulacrum ex ferro pendere in aere videretur. r Est qeippe alius in Æthiopia magnes, qui ferrum omne abigit, respuitque.
passages.english: It is rust-coloured, and it is tested when, placed next to iron, it seizes it. For it grips iron so strongly that it makes a chain of rings. Hence the common people also call it 'living iron'. It is also believed to draw the liquid of glass, as it does iron. Its power is so great (as the most blessed Augustine relates) that a certain man held this magnet stone under a silver vessel and placed iron on top of the silver; then, as his hand moved the stone underneath, the iron moved quickly above. Hence it came about that in a certain temple an image of iron seemed to hang in the air. There is indeed another magnet in Ethiopia, which drives away and repels all iron.
passages.notes: The text is badly scanned. The readings taken are: "Eit" as "Est"; "Med" as "sed"; "raptum" as "raptum" (perhaps "raptus"); "titri" as "vitri"; "creditnE" as "creditur"; "qeippe" as "quippe". The reading "liquid of glass" is uncertain.

passages.original: 19. m Ebur a barro, id est, elephante dictum. Horatius : Quid tibi vis, mulier, nigris dignissima barris?
passages.english: Ivory (*ebur*) is named from *barrus*, that is, the elephant. Horace: "What do you want, woman, most worthy of black elephants?"

passages.original: 1. Aurum d ab aura dictum, id est, a splendore, quod repercusso aere plus fulgeat. Unde et Virgilius : Discolor inde auri per ramos aura refulsit, hoc est, splendor auri. Naturale enim est ut metallorum splendor plus fulgeat luce alia repercussus. c Hinc et aurarii dicti, quorum fulgor splendidos reddit.
passages.english: Gold (*aurum*) is named from *aura*, that is, from its brightness, because it shines more when the air is reflected. Hence Virgil too: "Then the different-coloured gleam (*aura*) of gold shone back through the branches," that is, the brightness of gold. For it is natural that the brightness of metals shines more when struck by other light. Hence also those people whom its gleam renders splendid are called 'gilded' (*aurarii*).
passages.notes: The sense of "aurarii" here is uncertain.

passages.original: b Talentum autem summum esse pondus perbibetur in Graecis; 301 nam nihil est chalco minus, nihi! talento majus. c Cujus varium apud diversas gentes pondus habetur. Apud Romanos enim talentum est LXXII librarum , sicut Plautus ostendit, qui ait duo talenta esse CXLIV libras. Est autem triplex, id est, minus, medium, summum. Minus L, d medium LXXII libris, e summum cxx constat.
passages.english: The talent is held to be the greatest weight among the Greeks; for nothing is smaller than the *chalcus* and nothing greater than the talent. Its weight is reckoned variously among different peoples. Among the Romans the talent is 72 pounds, as Plautus shows, who says that two talents are 144 pounds. It is threefold, namely the lesser, the middle and the greatest. The lesser consists of 50 [pounds], the middle of 72 pounds, and the greatest of 120.
passages.notes: "perbibetur" is read as "perhibetur".

passages.original: i. Prima a Geres cœpit uti frugibus in Graecia, et habere segetes, translatis aliunde seminibus. Hujus meminit Ovidius dicens: Prima Ceres unco glebam dimovit aratro; I Prima dedi!. fruges, alimentaque mitia terris.
passages.english:
Ceres first began to use grain in Greece and to have crops, with seeds brought from elsewhere. Ovid mentions her, saying: "Ceres first turned the clod with the curved plough;
she first gave grain and gentle nourishment to the lands."
passages.notes: "Geres" is read as "Ceres" and "dedi!." as "dedit".

passages.original: 19. Palea a quibusdam vocari dicitur, quod pala ventiletur, ut frumenta purgentur. Gentiles autem paleam a quadam Pate frugum inventrice nominaverunt, quam Cererem esse volunt. De qua Virgilius:
passages.english: Chaff (*palea*) is said by some to be so called because it is winnowed with a shovel (*pala*), so that the grain may be cleaned. But the pagans named *palea* after a certain Pales, discoverer of crops, whom they hold to be Ceres. Of her Virgil [says]:
passages.notes: "Pate" is read as "Pale" (Pales). The quotation is missing from the passage.

passages.original: 10. 1 Vicia dicta, quod vix ad triplicem perveniat fructum, 316 cum alia legumina proventum habeant fertilem. Unde et Virgilius : Aut tenues fetus viciæ.
passages.english: 10. Vetch (vicia) is so called because it scarcely (vix) reaches a threefold yield, whereas other legumes have a fertile return. Hence also Virgil: "Or the slender offspring of the vetch."
passages.notes: "316" is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted, as is the initial "1".

passages.original: Hastula a tollendo nuncupata, quasi obstula. 0 Fomes est hastula quae ab arboribus excu titur recisione, aut hastulæ ambustæ, aut ligna cavata, a fungis nomine accepto, qnod ita capiat ignem. De quo Virgilius : Rapuitque in fomite flammam.
passages.english: A splinter (hastula) is named from lifting (tollendo), as if obstula. Tinder (fomes) is a splinter that is struck off from trees by cutting, or charred splinters, or hollowed wood; it takes its name from fungi, because it catches fire in this way. Of this Virgil [says]: "And he caught the flame in the tinder."
passages.notes: The stray "0" is omitted as a footnote mark. "excu titur" is read as excutitur and "qnod" as quod. The derivation "a fungis" is as transmitted; its logic (perhaps from fomes/fungus, or from foveo) is unclear.

passages.original: Nam Lucullus, cum Cerasum civitatem Ponti delesset, hoc genus pomi inde avexit, et a civitate Cerasum appellavit. Arbor autem Cerasus, pomum cerasum dicitur. Hoc etiam et ante Lucullum erat in Italia, sed durum, unde et Cornum appellatum est. Est autem arbor apta hastilibus, unde et Virgilius : Bona bello cornus.
passages.english: For Lucullus, when he had destroyed Cerasus, a city of Pontus, carried this kind of fruit away from there, and named it cerasus after the city. The tree, then, is called cerasus, and the fruit cerasum. This [tree] also existed in Italy before Lucullus, but hard, and so it was called cornus [cornel]. It is a tree suited to spear-shafts, hence also Virgil: "The cornel, good for war."
passages.notes: The passage conflates the cherry (cerasus) with the cornel (cornus), as the text stands.

passages.original: 25. Amygdala nomen Graecum est, e quae Latine nux longa vocatur. i Hanc alii nucidam vocant, quasi minorem nucem. De qua Virgilius : Cum se nux plurima sitvis induet in plorem. Cunctis enim arboribus prior se flore vestit, et ad ferenda poma arbusta sequentia prævenit.
passages.english: 25. Amygdala [almond] is a Greek name, which in Latin is called "long nut." Others call it nucida, as if a smaller nut. Of it Virgil [says]: "When the nut-tree in abundance clothes itself in the woods with blossom." For it clothes itself with flower before all trees, and anticipates the following trees in bearing fruit.
passages.notes: Stray "e" and "i" are omitted as footnote marks. "sitvis" is read as silvis and "plorem" as florem.

passages.original: 32. Abies dicta, quod prae caeteris arboribus longe eat, et in excelsum promineat. a Cujus natura expers est terreni humoris, ac proinde babilis atque levis habetur. De qua Virgilius : Et casus abies visura marinos, quia ex ea naves fiunt. Hanc quidam Gallicum vocant propter candorem. Est autem sine nedo.
passages.english: 32. The fir (abies) is so called because it goes (eat) far beyond (prae) other trees and towers aloft. Its nature is free of earthly moisture, and therefore it is considered nimble and light. Of it Virgil [says]: "And the fir that will see the hazards of the sea," because ships are made from it. Some call it Gallic because of its whiteness. It is also without knots.
passages.notes: The stray "a" is omitted as a footnote mark. "babilis" is read as habilis, "nedo" as nodo, and "casus" as casus (Virgil's "casus abies visura marinos"). "Gallicum" is as transmitted; the sense of the name is unclear.

passages.original: Cedrus, quam Graeci ϰέδρον vocant: quasi a ϰαεομένης δρυὸς vypov, id est, arboris humor ardentis, cujus folia ad cypressi similitudinem respondent. Lignum vero jucundi odoris est, et diu durans, nec a tinea unquam exterminatur. De qua Persius : Et cedro digna locutus. Scilicet propter durabilcm perpetuitatem. b Unde et in Templis propter diuturnitatem ex hoc ligno lacunaria fiunt. c Hujus ligni resina cedrea dicitur, quae in conservandis libris adeo est utilis, 335 ut perliti ex ea, nec tineas patiantur, nec tempore consenescant.
passages.english: The cedar (cedrus), which the Greeks call kedros, as if from the moisture (hygron) of a burning oak (kaiomenē drys), that is, the moisture of a burning tree. Its leaves correspond in likeness to the cypress. Its wood has a pleasant scent and lasts long, and it is never destroyed by the moth. Of it Persius [says]: "And having spoken things worthy of cedar," that is, because of its lasting permanence. Hence also in temples the coffered ceilings are made from this wood, because of its durability. The resin of this wood is called cedrea, and it is so useful in preserving books that books smeared with it neither suffer moths nor grow old with time.
passages.notes: The Greek "vypov" is read as ὑγρόν (moisture), and the case forms of the Greek are garbled in the scan. "durabilcm" is read as durabilem. The stray "b", "c" and "335" are omitted as footnote marks and a page number.

passages.original: Cujus lignum nigrum est, et cortex levis, ut lauri, sed i Indicum maculosum est in parvulis distinctionibus albis ac fulvis. Æthiopicum vero, quod præstantius accipitur, in nullo est 336 maculatum, sed est nigrum, leve et corneum. k Est autem Mareotica palus in India, unde ebenus venit. 1 Lucanus : Ebenus Mareotica, inquit. Ebenus autem crepundiis illigatur, ut infantem risu nigra non terreant.
passages.english: Its wood is black, and its bark smooth, like the laurel's. The Indian [kind] is spotted with tiny white and tawny markings. The Ethiopian, however, which is considered superior, is spotted nowhere, but is black, smooth and horn-like. There is also the Mareotic marsh in India, whence ebony comes. Lucan says: "Mareotic ebony." Ebony is also bound onto rattles, so that black things do not frighten an infant by their look.
passages.notes: "ut infantem risu nigra non terreant" is odd. The sense may be "so that, being black, they may not frighten the infant, [but amuse it] with laughter"; the text may be corrupt. Isidore wrongly places Lake Mareotis (in Egypt) in India. The stray letters and "336" are omitted as footnote marks and a page number.

passages.original: 39. Fraxinus vocari fertur, quod magis in asperis locis montanisque fragis nascatur. Hinc per derivationem fraxinus, sicut a monte montanas. De quo Ovidius: Et fraxinus utilis hastis.
passages.english: 39. The ash (fraxinus) is said to be so called because it grows mostly in rough and mountainous broken places (fragis). Hence by derivation fraxinus, just as montanus from mons. Of it Ovid [says]: "And the ash, useful for spears."
passages.notes: "fragis" is read as fragosis (rugged). "montanas" is read as montanus.

passages.original: 50. Myrtus a mari dicta, eo quod magis littorea arbor sit. Unde ei Virgilius : Littora myrtetis lætissima; et : Amantes littora myrtos. llinc est, quod a Græci. μυρίνη dicitur. i Medicorum autem libri hanc arborem aptam scribunt mulierum necessitatibas plurimis.
passages.english: 50. The myrtle (myrtus) is named from the sea (mare), because it is chiefly a shore tree. Hence also Virgil: "Shores most delightful with myrtle-groves"; and: "Myrtles loving the shores." This is why it is called myrinē by the Greeks. The books of physicians write that this tree is suited to very many needs of women.
passages.notes: "ei" is read as et, "llinc" as Hinc, "Græci." as Græcis, and "necessitatibas" as necessitatibus.

passages.original: 51. Lentitcus, quod cuspis ipsius lenta sit, et motlis. Nam lentum dicimus quidquid flexibile est, unde et lentum vimen, et vites, Virgilius: Et tentæ vites, pro flexibiles. k Hujus fructus oleum desudat, cortex rcsinam, quæ mastix appellatur, cujus plurima et melior in Ghio insula gignitur.
passages.english: 51. The mastic tree (lentiscus) [is so called] because its point is pliant (lenta) and soft. For we call lentum whatever is flexible, whence also "pliant osier," and vines; Virgil: "And pliant vines," for "flexible." Its fruit exudes oil, and its bark a resin which is called mastix; the most and the best of it is produced on the island of Chios.
passages.notes: Scanning errors are corrected: Lentiscus, mollis, lentæ, resinam and Chio. The stray "k" is omitted as a footnote mark.

passages.original: 74. a Omnia poma Latine neutri generis esse die cuntur; arbores autem feminini sunt generis, exceptis paucis, ut hic oleaster, hoc siler, ut Virgilius : Molle siler. Item hoc buxum, licet et hæc buxus dicatur. Nam superfluam quidam volunt facere discretionem, ut hæc buxus de arbore dicamus, buxum vero de ligno composito.
passages.english: 74.
