All fruits are said in Latin to be of the neuter gender; trees, however, are of the feminine gender, with a few exceptions, such as hic oleaster [wild olive, masculine] and hoc siler [osier, neuter], as Virgil [has]: "the soft osier." Likewise hoc buxum [box, neuter], although it is also called haec buxus [feminine]. For some want to make a superfluous distinction, so that we say haec buxus of the tree, but buxum of the worked wood.
passages.notes: Leading 'a' is a footnote mark; 'die cuntur' read as 'dicuntur'.

passages.original: 12. Thymum appellatum, quod flos ejus odorern refert. Dequo Virgilius : Redolentque thymo fragrat. tia mella.
passages.english: 12. Thyme (thymum) is so called because its flower gives off a scent. Of it Virgil [says]: "And the fragrant honey smells of thyme."
passages.notes: 'odorern' read as 'odorem', 'fragrat. tia' as 'fragrantia'. The etymology presumably rests on Greek thymos/thyein (incense, burning); the text does not make it explicit.

passages.original: 14. h Sampsuchus est, quem Latini amaracum vocant. Cujus nominis usum Virgilius etiam ad Yenerem referens ait : Ubi mollis amaracus illum Floribus, et dulci aspirans complectitur umbra. Apta est autem haec herba unguentis. i Unde et no. men traxit amaracus a puero cujusdam regis, qui casu lapsus dum ferret unguenta , novum et gratissimum ex confusione odorem creavit.
passages.english: 14. Sampsuchus is [the plant] which the Latins call amaracus [marjoram]. Virgil, applying the use of this name also to Venus, says: "Where soft marjoram embraces him with its flowers and sweet-breathing shade." This herb is suited to unguents. Hence too amaracus took its name from the boy of a certain king, who fell by accident while carrying unguents and, by their mixing, created a new and most pleasing scent.
passages.notes: Footnote marks 'h' and 'i' omitted; 'Yenerem' read as 'Venerem'. Virgil's line actually refers to Ascanius ('illum'), not Venus; Isidore's phrasing is loose.

passages.original: 22. s Hedera dicta , quod arboribus reptando adhæreat. De qua Virgilius : Inter viclrices hederam tibi serpere lauros. Alii hederam 352 aiunt vocatam, t quod hædis supra lactis abundantiam in escam a veteribus præbebatur.
passages.english: 22. Ivy (hedera) is so called because it clings (adhaereat) to trees by creeping. Of it Virgil [says]: "[that] the ivy creeps for you among the victorious laurels." Others say ivy was so named because it was given by the ancients as food to kids (haedis), on top of their abundance of milk.
passages.notes: Marks 's', 't' and page number 352 omitted; 'viclrices' read as 'victrices'.

passages.original: 29. Dycta est mons Cretae, ex quo dyctamnum herba nomen accepit, propter quam apud Virgilium cerva vulnerata saltus peragrat Dyctæos. Tantæ enim potentiæ est, ut ferrum a corpore expellat, sagittas excutiat ; unde et ejus pabnlo feræ percussae sagit- Usa corpore inhærentes ejiciunt. f Hanc quidam Laiinorum poleium Martis dicunt propter belli tela excutienda.
passages.english: 29. Dicte is a mountain of Crete, from which the herb dittany (dictamnum) took its name; on account of it, in Virgil, the wounded doe roams the Dictaean glades. For it is of such power that it drives iron out of the body and shakes out arrows; hence wild beasts struck [by arrows], by grazing on it, expel the arrows lodged in their body. Some of the Latins call it 'pennyroyal of Mars', because it shakes out the weapons of war.
passages.notes: 'pabnlo' read as 'pabulo', 'sagit- Usa' as 'sagittas'; mark 'f' omitted. Virgil's 'Dictaeos' saltus is actually of Dido-simile deer in Aeneid 4; spelling Dycta for Dicte kept as name.

passages.original: 31. 1 Papuver herba somnifera. De qua Virgilius : Lethæo perfusa papavera somno. Soporem enim languentibus facit. Ejus alia est usualis, alia agrestis, ex qua fluit m succus, quem opium appellant.
passages.english: 31. The poppy is a sleep-bringing herb. Of it Virgil [says]: "poppies steeped in Lethean sleep." For it brings slumber to the sick. One kind of it is cultivated, another wild, from which flows a juice which they call opium.
passages.notes: 'Papuver' read as 'Papaver'; marks '1' and 'm' omitted.

passages.original: 48. e Pæon quidam medicus fuit, a quo Pæonia berba perhibetur inventa, ut Homerus dicit. Hanc quidam glycysiden vocant, quod dulcis saporis sit, vel pentorobon a numero granorum, vel, ut alii, dactylosam a digitorum similitudine. Nascitur in silvis.
passages.english: 48. Paeon was a certain physician, by whom the herb paeonia [peony] is said to have been discovered, as Homer says. Some call it glycyside, because it has a sweet taste, or pentorobon, from the number of its seeds, or, as others [say], dactylosa, from its resemblance to fingers. It grows in woods.
passages.notes: Mark 'e' omitted; 'berba' read as 'herba'.

passages.original: 71. Cicuta propter quod in thyrso geniculato nodos habeat occultos, ut canna; sic dicitur fossa ceca, quæ occulta est. Hæc potui data interficit. Hanc In canere Socrates bibit, et expiravit. Persius : Dicere, sorbitio tollit quem dira cicutæ. Hæc dum hominibus venenum sit, capellas efficit pingucs.
passages.english: 71. Hemlock (cicuta) [is so called] because in its jointed stalk it has hidden knots, like a reed; thus a hidden ditch is called 'blind' (caeca). Given as a drink, it kills. Socrates drank it in prison and died. Persius: "Say [it], you whom a dire draught of hemlock carries off." Although it is poison to men, it makes she-goats fat.
passages.notes: 'In canere' read as 'in carcere' (in prison); 'pingucs' as 'pingues'. The etymology (cicuta from caecus) is implied, not stated.

passages.original: 80. Ambrosia, quam Latini Aptum sylvaticum vocant. De qua Virgilius : Ambrosiaeque comae divinum vertice odorem Spiravere.....
passages.english: 80. Ambrosia, which the Latins call wild apium [celery/parsley]. Of it Virgil [says]: "And her ambrosial locks breathed a divine fragrance from her head....."
passages.notes: 'Aptum' read as 'apium'. Text breaks off after the quotation.

passages.original: 95. r Ferula vocata a medulla. Nam illam Varro tradit esse ferulae medullam, quam ἀπόδερον Gr:rci vocant. Nonnulli a feriendo 364 ferulam dicunt. Hac enim pueri et puellæ vapulare solent : s hujus succus galbanum est.
passages.english: 95. Fennel-giant (ferula) is named from its pith. For Varro records that what the Greeks call apoderon is the pith of the ferula. Some say ferula comes from striking (ferire), for boys and girls are customarily beaten with it. Its juice is galbanum.
passages.notes: Greek 'apoderon' uncertain as printed.

passages.original: 97. u Scirpus, a quo tegetes texuntur sine nudo, de quo Ennius : Quaerunt in scirpo soliti quod dicere nodum. Et in proverbio : Qui inimicus est, etiam in scirpo bodum quærit.
passages.english: 97. The bulrush (scirpus), from which mats are woven without a knot; of which Ennius [says]: "They seek, as they are wont to say, a knot in a bulrush." And in the proverb: "Whoever is hostile looks for a knot even in a bulrush."
passages.notes: 'nudo' and 'bodum' read as 'nodo', 'nodum'.

passages.original: 98. v Fucus genus herbae eit, de qua tingitur vestis : x dicta quia mentitur alienum colorem ; unde et Virgilius : Discet mentiri lana color..
passages.english: 98. Fucus is a kind of herb with which clothing is dyed; it is so called because it counterfeits a colour not its own; hence also Virgil: "Wool will learn to counterfeit colour."
passages.notes: Marks 'v', 'x' omitted; 'eit' read as 'est'. Virgil's line reads 'varios mentiri lana colores'; the quotation here is garbled.

passages.original: 102. a Carex acuta herba et durissima, sparto similis, de qua Virgilius : Et carice pastus acuta.
passages.english: 102. Sedge (*carex*) is a sharp and very hard plant, similar to esparto, about which Virgil [says]: "And fed on sharp sedge."
passages.notes: The "a" before Carex is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Justum bellum est, quod ex prædicto geritur de rebus repelitis, aut propulsandorum hostium causa. Injustum bellum est, quod de furore, non de legitima ratione initur. De quo in Republica dicit Cicero : Illa injusta bella sunt, quæ sunt sine causa suscepta.
passages.english: A just war is one that is waged after a declaration, concerning property sought back, or for the sake of repelling enemies. An unjust war is one that is begun from rage, not from lawful reason. Concerning this Cicero says in the Republic: "Those wars are unjust which are undertaken without cause."
passages.notes: "repelitis" read as "repetitis" (things demanded back).

passages.original: Plusquam civile bellum est, ubi non solum cives certant, sed et cognati: quale actum est inter Cæsarem et Pompeium, quando gener et socer invicem dimicaverunt. Siquidem in hac pugna frater cum fratre dimicavit, et pater adversus filium arma portavit. 372 Lucanus : In fratrem ceciderunt prœnia fratris. Item : Cui cervix cæsa parentis cederet.
passages.english: A more than civil war is one where not only citizens fight, but also kinsmen: such as was waged between Caesar and Pompey, when son-in-law and father-in-law fought against each other. Indeed in this fight brother fought with brother, and father bore arms against son. Lucan: "Brothers fell as the prizes of brothers." Likewise: "To whom the severed neck of a parent would fall."
passages.notes: "prœnia" read as "praemia". "372" is a page number, omitted. The second Lucan line is garbled in this form and translated literally.

passages.original: 7. Quo autem differat utrumque, d Cicero docet: Po. test enim, inquit, esse bellum, ut tumultus non sit. e Tumultus autem esse sine bello non potest. Quid est enim tumultus,nisi perturbatio tanta, ut major timor oriatur? Unde etiam dictus tumultus, quasi timor multus. Gravior autem est tumultus quali bellum. Nam in bello vacaliones valent, in tumultu non valent.
passages.english: 7. How the two differ Cicero teaches: "For there can be war," he says, "without there being a *tumultus* [emergency]. But a *tumultus* cannot exist without war." For what is a *tumultus* but a disturbance so great that a greater fear arises? Hence it is also called *tumultus*, as if *timor multus* [much fear]. A *tumultus* is more serious than a war. For in war exemptions [from service] are valid; in a *tumultus* they are not valid.
passages.notes: Footnote marks "d" and "e" omitted; "quali" read as "quam", "vacaliones" as "vacationes".

passages.original: Fædu est pavI quæ fit inter dimicantes, vel a (ide, vel a facialibus, id cst, sacerdotibus dictum. Per ipsos enim fiebant fædera, sicut per sæculares bella. b Alia fœdera dicta putant a porca fœde et cru- deliter occisa, cujus mors optabatur ei qui a pace resilisset. Virgilius: Et cœsa jungebant fœdera porca. Fœderis partes induciæ. Et dictæ induciæ, quasi in dies ocia.
passages.english: A treaty (*foedus*) is a peace made between those who have been fighting, named either from "faith" (*fides*) or from the *fetiales*, that is, priests. For treaties were made through them, just as wars [were made] through laymen. Others think treaties were named from a sow killed foully (*foede*) and cruelly, whose death was invoked upon anyone who withdrew from the peace. Virgil: "And they joined treaties with a slaughtered sow." Parts of a treaty are truces (*induciae*). And they are called *induciae* as if "leisure (*otia*) into days."
passages.notes: Corrupt OCR read as: "Foedus est pax, quae fit ... vel a fide, vel a fetialibus, id est".

passages.original: Nam turpis est dulu quæsita victoria. Certa autem victoria est, vel occisio hostis, vel exspoliatio, vel utrumque. c Non est autem jucunda victoria, 374 quæ per immensa detrimenta contingit. Est hoc est, quod laudat Sallustius duces victoriam in cruento exercitu reportasse.
passages.english: For a victory sought by deceit is shameful. A certain victory is either the killing of the enemy, or their despoiling, or both. But a victory that comes through immense losses is not pleasing. And this is why Sallust praises generals who brought back victory with a bloodless army.
passages.notes: "dulu" read as "dolo"; "Est hoc est" as "Et hoc est"; "in cruento" read as "incruento" (bloodless), as the sense requires. "374" page number omitted.

passages.original: i. Duobus autem generibus deletur exercitus, aul internecione, aut dispersione. Sallustius: Hostes, inquit, aut oppressi, aut dilapsi forent. Sic et utrumque Virgilius : internecione, ut: Submersasque obrue puppes; dispersione, ut : Aut age diversos, et disjice corpora ponto.
passages.english: 1. An army is destroyed in two ways, either by slaughter or by dispersal. Sallust says: "The enemies would have been either crushed or scattered." So Virgil too [has] both: slaughter, as in "And overwhelm the sunken ships"; dispersal, as in "Or drive them apart and scatter their bodies over the sea."

passages.original: a Nam dum idem Jovis adversus Tita- nas proficisceretur, aquilam ei in auspicio apparuisse ferunt, quam ille pro indicio victoriæ acceptam tutelæ suae auspicatus eam legioni signum dedit, quo factum est ut deinceps militum signa comitaretur. Cujus meminit Lucanus dicens : Signa pares aquilas, et pila minantia pilis
passages.english: For when that same Jupiter was setting out against the Titans, they say an eagle appeared to him in an augury; he accepted it as a sign of victory, and having taken it as the omen of his protection, he gave it to the legion as a standard, whence it came about that afterwards it accompanied the standards of soldiers. Lucan mentions it, saying: "Standards matching standards, eagles alike, and javelins threatening javelins."
passages.notes: Lucan's line here is truncated; the usual text begins "signa pares aquilas" ("standards, matching eagles"). Footnote mark "a" omitted.

passages.original: 1. Buccina est qua signum dalur in hostem, dicta a voce, quasi vocina. Nam pagani agrestesque ad omnem Usum buccina ad compita convocabantur. Proprie ergo hoc agrestibus signum fuit. De qua Propertius : Buccina jam priscos cogebat ad arma Quiriles. d Hujus clangor buccinum dicilur.
passages.english: 1. The *buccina* [horn] is that by which the signal is given against the enemy, named from the voice (*vox*), as if *vocina*. For villagers and country folk were called together to the crossroads by the *buccina* for every purpose. Properly, then, this was a signal for country people. About it Propertius [says]: "The horn was then summoning the ancient Quirites to arms." Its blast is called *buccinum*.
passages.notes: Footnote mark "d" omitted.

passages.original: 2. c Tubam Tyrrheni primum invenerunt, unde Virgilius : Tyrrbenusque tubae mugire per aethera clangor.
passages.english: 2. The Tyrrhenians first invented the trumpet, whence Virgil [says]: "And the Tyrrhenian blare of the trumpet bellowed through the air."

passages.original: 5. i Classica sunt cornua, quae convocandi causa erant facta, et a calando classica dicebantur. De quibus Virgilius : Classica jamque sonant. k Apud Amazonas autem non tuba sicut a regibus, sed a regina sistro vocabatur feminarum exercitus.
passages.english: 5. *Classica* are horns which were made for the purpose of calling [men] together, and they were called *classica* from *calare* [to call]. Of these Virgil [says]: "And now the *classica* sound." Among the Amazons, however, the army of women was summoned not by a trumpet, as [armies are] by kings, but by the queen with a sistrum.
passages.notes: Stray letters "i" and "k" are footnote marks and are omitted.

passages.original: 5. Trudes hastæ sunt cum lunato ferro, quae Græ- eis aplustria dicuntur. Trudes autem dicuntur ab eo quod trudunt, et detrudunt. Virgilius : Ferratasque trudes.
passages.english: 5. *Trudes* are spears with a crescent-shaped iron [head], which among the Greeks are called *aplustria*. They are called *trudes* from the fact that they thrust (*trudunt*) and thrust down. Virgil: "And iron-tipped *trudes*."
passages.notes: "Græ- eis" read as "Græcis". The identification of *trudes* with Greek *aplustria* (properly a ship's stern ornament) is odd and may reflect a textual problem.

passages.original: 7. I Clava est, qualis fuit Herculis dicta, quod sit clavis ferreis invicem religata, x ei est cubito semis facta in longitudine. h Hæc et cateja, quam Lucilius calam dicit. Est enim genus Gallici teli ex materia quam maxime lenta, quæ jacta quidem non longa propter gravitatem evolat ; sed quo pervenit, vi nimia perfringit : quod si ab artifice mittatur, rursum I redit ad eum qui misit. Hujus meminit Virgilius, dicens : Teutooico ritu soliti torquere catejas Unde et eos i Hispani et Galli Teutonos vocant.
passages.english: 7. The club (clava), such as that of Hercules was, is so called because it is bound together with iron nails (clavi), and it is made a cubit and a half in length. This is also the cateia, which Lucilius calls cala. For it is a kind of Gallic missile made of very pliant wood, which when thrown does not fly far because of its weight, but where it arrives it smashes through with great force; and if it is thrown by a skilled man, it returns again to the one who threw it. Virgil mentions it, saying: "accustomed to hurl cateias in the Teutonic manner." Hence the Spaniards and Gauls also call them Teutoni.
passages.notes: The final sentence is abrupt; the referent of 'eos' is unclear in the excerpt. Stray letters omitted.

passages.original: i Phalarica est telum ingens torno factum, habens ferrum 383 cubitale, et rolunditatem de plumbo in modum sphæræ in ipsa summitate. Dicitur etiam et ignem habere affixum. Hoc aulem lelo pugnatur de turribus, quas phalas dici manifestum est. Juvenalis : Consulit aute pbalas, delphinorumqua columnas. A phalis igitur dicta est phalerica, sicut a muro muralis. Sane phalaricam Lucanus dicit nervis mitti tortilibus, et quadam machina, ut : Hunc aut tortilibus vibrata phalarica nervis. Yirgilius vero ait Turnum manu phalaricam jaculari potuisse.
passages.english: The *phalarica* is a huge spear made on a lathe, having an iron [head] a cubit long, and a round mass of lead in the shape of a ball at its very tip. It is also said to have fire attached to it. This weapon is used for fighting from towers, which it is clear are called *phalae*. Juvenal: "He consults the *phalae* beforehand, and the columns of dolphins." So the *phalarica* is named from *phalae*, as *muralis* [of a wall] from *murus* [wall]. Lucan indeed says that the *phalarica* is launched by twisted sinews and by some kind of machine, as: "This one, the *phalarica* hurled by twisted sinews." Virgil, however, says that Turnus was able to hurl a *phalarica* by hand.
passages.notes: The "383" is a page number and the opening "i" a footnote mark; both are omitted. Scanning errors are corrected: rolunditatem → rotunditatem, aulem lelo → autem telo, aute pbalas → ante phalas, delphinorumqua → delphinorumque, Yirgilius → Virgilius.

passages.original: ii. Cuspis hastile amentatum, a cespite dicta, quod est virgultum. Virgilius : Et pastoralem præfixa cuspide myrtum. e Proprie autem cuspis, pustenor pars hastæ est.
passages.english: The *cuspis* is a spear-shaft fitted with a throwing-thong, named from *cespes*, which is a shrub. Virgil: "And a shepherd's myrtle [staff] with a point (*cuspis*) fixed on." Properly, however, the *cuspis* is the rear part of the spear.
passages.notes: "pustenor" read as "posterior". The stray "e" is a footnote mark.

passages.original: 5. b Ancile vocatur scutum breve et rotundum. De quo Virgilios : Lævaque ancile gerebat. Et Ancile dictum ab ancisione, quod sit ab omni parte veluti ancisum et rotundum. Ovidius : Idque ancile vocant, quod ab omni parte recisum. Quaque notes oculis, angulus omnis abest.
passages.english: 5. The *ancile* is the name for a short, round shield. Of it Virgil [says]: "And in his left [hand] he carried the *ancile*." And *ancile* is named from *ancisio* [cutting around], because it is as if cut around on every side and rounded. Ovid: "And they call it *ancile*, because it is cut away on every side; and wherever you look with your eyes, every angle is absent."
passages.notes: "Virgilios" read as "Virgilius".

passages.original: Dicitur autem et testudo scutum. Nam in modum testudinis fit clypeus. 388 f Est et testudo scutorum connexio curvata in testudinis modum. Namque in armorum generibus, milites etiam ab animalibus nomina sumunt, ut aries. Et Sallustius : In modum, inquit, hericii militaris.
passages.english: A shield is also called a *testudo* [tortoise]. For the shield is made in the shape of a tortoise. There is also the *testudo* as a joining of shields, curved in the manner of a tortoise. For among the kinds of arms, soldiers also take names from animals, such as the ram. And Sallust says: "In the manner of a military hedgehog."
passages.notes: The "388" is a page number and the "f" a footnote mark; both are omitted.

passages.original: Lis a contentione limitis prius nomen sumpsi. De quo Virgilius: Limes erat positus, litem ut i discerneret agri.
passages.english: *Lis* [lawsuit] first took its name from a dispute over a *limes* [boundary]. Of which Virgil [says]: "A boundary stone had been set, to settle a dispute over the field."
passages.notes: "sumpsi" read as "sumpsit".

passages.original: Igitur in Etruria inter cæteros ritus superstitionum suarum, spectacula quoquo religionis nomine instituerunt. Inde Romani accersitos artifices mutuati sunt, et inde ludi a Lydis vocati sunt. Varro autem dicit ludos a lusu voca. ius, quod juvenes per dies festos solebant ludi exsultatione delectare populum. Unde et eum lusumjuvenum, et diebus festis, et templis, et religionibus reputat.
passages.english: So in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, they established spectacles under some name of religion. From there the Romans summoned craftsmen and borrowed [them], and so the games (ludi) were named from the Lydians. Varro, however, says that ludi were named from play (lusus), because on feast days young men used to delight the people with the exuberance of play. Hence he regards that play of the young men as belonging to feast days, to temples and to religious rites.
passages.notes: 'voca. ius' is a scanning error for 'vocatos'; 'quoquo' read as 'quodam' or 'quoquo' (in some name). 'ludi exsultatione' read as 'ludi' (of play) or possibly 'lusus'.

passages.original: 2. Itaque et Castori et Polluci deputuntur hæ species, quibus equos a Mercurio distributos Stesichorus docet; sed et Neptunus equestris est, quem Græci Hippion appellant; sed et Marti et Jovi in ludis equi sunt consecrati, et ipsi quadrigis præsunt.
passages.english: And so these kinds [of contests] are assigned to Castor and Pollux, to whom, Stesichorus teaches, horses were allotted by Mercury; but Neptune too is equestrian, whom the Greeks call Hippios; and horses in the games are also consecrated to Mars and Jupiter, and they themselves preside over four-horse chariots.
passages.notes: 'deputuntur' read as 'deputantur'. 'Hippion' is the Greek accusative of Hippios.

passages.original: i. e Ericthonius autem, qui regnavit Athenis, primus quatuor equos junxisse fertur, sicut Virgilius auctor est dicens : Primos Ericthonius currus, et quatuor ausus Jungere equos, rapidisque rotis insistere victor.
passages.english: Erichthonius, who reigned at Athens, is said to have been the first to yoke four horses together, as Virgil is the authority, saying: "Erichthonius first dared to yoke chariots and four horses, and to stand victorious upon swift wheels."

passages.original: 3. Ideo autem rotis quadrigas currere dicunt, sive quia mundus iste circuli sui celeritate transcurrit, sive propter solem, quia volubili ambitu rotat, sicut ait Ennius : j Inde patefecit radiis rola candida caelum.
passages.english: They say that four-horse chariots run on wheels either because this world passes swiftly through the speed of its circuit, or on account of the sun, because it turns in a revolving circuit, as Ennius says: "Then the bright wheel opened the sky with its rays."
passages.notes: Stray 'j' omitted; 'rola' read as 'rota'.

passages.original: i. Saltarores b autem nominatos Varro dicit ab Arcade Salio, quem Æneas in Italiam secum adduxit, quique primo docuit Romanos adolescentes nobiles saltare.
passages.english: Varro says that dancers (saltatores) were named after the Arcadian Salius, whom Aeneas brought with him into Italy, and who first taught noble Roman youths to dance.
passages.notes: 'Saltarores' read as 'Saltatores'; stray 'b' and section numeral omitted.

passages.original: 12. n Liburnæ dictæ a Libyis ; naves enim sunt negotiatorum. De quibus Horatius : Ibis liburnis inter alta navium.
passages.english: 12. *Liburnae* are named from the Libyans; for they are merchants' ships. Of them Horace [says]: "You will go in Liburnian [galleys] among the lofty [bulwarks] of ships."
passages.notes: The derivation from "Libyans" (rather than the Liburnians of Illyria) is as given in the text.

passages.original: 17. Phasclus est navigium quod nos corrupte baselum dicimus. De quo Virgilius : Putisque phaselis.
passages.english: 17. The *phaselus* is a vessel which we, in a corrupt form, call *baselus*. Of it Virgil [says]: "And with painted *phaseli*."
passages.notes: "Phasclus" read as "Phaselus". "Putisque" is probably an error for "pictisque" (painted).

passages.original: 20. r Paro navigium piratarum aptum, et ex iis ita vocatum, Cicero : Tunc se fluctigero tradit, mandatque paroni Et alibi : Parunculis ad littus ludit celeribus.
passages.english: The paro is a boat suited to pirates, and named after them [i.e. as theirs]. Cicero: "Then he entrusts himself to the wave-bearing [sea], and commits himself to a paro." And elsewhere: "He sports by the shore in swift little parones."
passages.notes: The initial "r" is a footnote mark, omitted. The etymology "ex iis" presumably refers to the pirates, though the derivation is unclear.

passages.original: 22. Celoces, a quas Graeci ϰέλητας vocant, id est, veloces biremes , vel triremes agiles, et ad ministerium classis aptæ. Ennius : Labitur uncla carina per æquora cana celocis.
passages.english: Celoces, which the Greeks call kelētes, that is, swift biremes or nimble triremes, fit for the service of a fleet. Ennius: "The greased keel of the celox glides over the white seas."
passages.notes: Footnote mark 'a' omitted; 'uncla' read as 'uncta'.

passages.original: De quibus Virgilius : Laxatque foros.
passages.english: About which Virgil [says]: "and he loosens the gangways."
passages.notes: Without context, the referent of "quibus" (presumably the fori, a ship's gangways or decks) is uncertain.

passages.original: 5. Transtra sunt tabulae ubi sedent remiges, quod in transverso sint, dicta, n quae Virgilius juga appellat.
passages.english: Transtra are the planks where the rowers sit, so called because they are set crosswise; Virgil calls them juga.
passages.notes: The stray "n" is a footnote mark, omitted.

passages.original: 11. Parastatæ stipites sunt pares stante?, quibus arbor sustinetur. Cato : Malum deligatum, parastatæ vincla.
passages.english: Parastatae are paired standing posts by which the mast is supported. Cato: "The mast tied fast, the parastatae [as] bindings."
passages.notes: "stante?" is read as "stantes". The Cato quotation is fragmentary and its syntax is uncertain.

passages.original: 12. a Clavus est quo regitur gubernaculum. De quo Ennius : . Ut clavum rectum teneam, navimque gobernem.
passages.english: The clavus is that by which the rudder is steered. Of it Ennius [says]: "That I may hold the tiller straight and steer the ship."
passages.notes: 'gobernem' read as 'gubernem'.

passages.original: 13. b Porticulus malleus in manu portatus, quo tnodus signumque datur remigantibus. De quo Plautus : Ad loquendum, atque ad tacendum tote habeas porti- culum.] A portando igitur porticulus.
passages.english: The porticulus is a hammer carried in the hand, by which the stroke and signal are given to those rowing. About it Plautus [says]: "For speaking and for keeping silent, you hold the porticulus entirely." So porticulus [comes] from portare [to carry].
passages.notes: "tnodus" is read as "modus" (the beat or measure). "tote" is likely corrupt (perhaps "tute", 'you yourself'). The stray "b" is a footnote mark, and the bracket "]" is an edition sign; both are omitted.

passages.original: 423 4. Siparum genus veli, anum pedetn habens, quo juvari navigia solent iN navigatione, quoties tis venti languescit. De quo Lucanus: Summaque tendens Sipara, velorum perituras colligit auras, quod ex separatione existimant nominatum. h Pes exiremus angulus veli, quem sic nautæ loquuntur.
passages.english: The siparum is a kind of sail with a single foot, by which ships are usually helped in sailing whenever the force of the wind slackens. About it Lucan [says]: "and stretching the topmost sipara, he gathers the dying breezes of the sails." They think it is named from separatio [separation]. The foot is the lowest corner of the sail, as sailors call it.
passages.notes: "423" is a page number, and the stray "h" is a footnote mark; both are omitted. The following corrections are adopted: "anum pedetn" as "unum pedem", "iN" as "in", "tis" as "vis", and "exiremus" as "extremus".

passages.original: 9. a Struppi, vincula loro vel lino facta, quibus remi ad scalmos alligantur. De quibus Livius: Tuncque remos jussit deligare struppis.
passages.english: Struppi are bindings made of leather or flax, by which oars are tied to the tholes. About them Livius [says]: "And then he ordered [them] to tie the oars with struppi."
passages.notes: The stray "a" is a footnote mark, omitted. "Livius" is probably Livius Andronicus.

passages.original: 10. b Catapirates linea cum massa plumbea , qua maris altitudo tentatur. 425 Lucilius : Hunc catapiratem pner eodem deferat unctum Plumbi pauxillum rodus, linique mataxam.
passages.english: The catapirates is a line with a lead weight by which the depth of the sea is tested. Lucilius: "Let the boy bring down this greased sounding-line to the same place, a little scrap of lead, and a hank of flax."
passages.notes: 'pner' read as 'puer'; '425' is a page number and omitted. The Lucilius fragment is obscure; 'rodus' (rudus, a lump) is uncertain.

passages.original: 2. Funda genus est piscatoriæ retis , dicta ab eo quod in fundum mittatur. e Eadem etiam a jactando jaculum dicitur. Plautus : Probus quidem antea jaculator eras.
passages.english: The funda is a kind of fishing net, so called because it is sent to the bottom (fundus). The same is also called jaculum from jactare [to throw]. Plautus: "You were indeed a good net-caster before."
passages.notes: The stray "e" is a footnote mark, omitted.

passages.original: Marcus malleus major, et dictus marcus , quod major sit ad cædendum, et fortior. d Martellus, mediocris Marculus, malleus pusillus. Lucilius : Et velut in fabricam fervens cum marculus ferrum multorum magnis ictibus tundit.
passages.english: The marcus is a larger hammer, and it is called marcus because it is larger for striking, and stronger. The martellus [is] medium-sized; the marculus a small hammer. Lucilius: "And as when in a workshop the glowing little hammer pounds the iron with many great blows."
passages.notes: The quotation is attributed to Lucilius; its wording seems disordered, with 'fervens' probably going with the iron.

passages.original: Laquearia f sunt quæ cameram subtegunt et ornant, quæ et lacunaria dicuntur, quod lacus quosdam quadratos, vel rotundos, ligno, vel gypso, vel coloribus, habeant pictos, cum siguis intermicantibus. Principaliter autem lacus dicitur, ut Lucilius : Resultant cedesque, lacusque. Cujus diminutio lacunar facit, ut . Horatius : Neque aureum Mea renidet in domo lacunar. Inde fit alia diminutio lacunarium, et per antistichon laquearium.
passages.english: Laquearia are what cover and adorn a vaulted ceiling. They are also called lacunaria because they have certain square or round hollows (lacus) painted in wood, plaster or colours, with figures gleaming among them. Originally, however, it is called lacus, as Lucilius [says]: "Both the halls and the panels resound." Its diminutive makes lacunar, as Horace [says]: "Nor does a golden panelled ceiling shine in my house." From this comes a further diminutive, lacunarium, and by substitution of a letter (antistichon), laquearium.
passages.notes: 'siguis' read as 'signis'; 'cedesque' probably 'aedesque' (halls). Footnote marks omitted.

passages.original: Acupicla vestis, acu textilis, vel acu ornata. a Eadem et Phrygia. Hujus enim artis periti Phrygii omnes dicuntur; sive quia in Phrygia inventa est. Unde et artifices, qui id faciunt, Phrygiones dicuntur. Virgilius: Phrygiam Aacanio chlamydem.
passages.english: Acupicta is a garment woven with the needle, or adorned with the needle. The same is also [called] Phrygian. For all those skilled in this art are called Phrygians; or [it is so called] because it was invented in Phrygia. Hence also the craftsmen who make it are called Phrygiones. Virgil: "a Phrygian cloak for Ascanius."
passages.notes: "Acupicla" is read as "Acupicta", and "Aacanio" as "Ascanio". The stray "a" is a footnote mark, omitted.

passages.original: 5. Lenæ, saga quadra et mollia sont. De quibus Plautus : Leua cooperta est textrina Gallia.
passages.english: 5. *Lenae* are square and soft cloaks. Of these Plautus [says]: "She is covered with a *lena*, a Gallic weave."
passages.notes: "sont" is read as "sunt" and "Leua" as "Lena" (scanning errors). The quoted line is obscure and probably corrupt; the rendering "a Gallic weave" for "textrina Gallia" is tentative. *Lena* is a heavy woollen cloak.

passages.original: Rhenones sunt velamina humerorum et pectoris usque 454 ad umbilicum, atque intortis villis adeo hispida, ut imbres respuant, quos vulgo reptos vocant, eo quod longitudo villorum, quasi reptat. De quibus Sallustius: Germani intectum rhenonibus corpus tegunt. Dicti autem q rhenonea a ltheno Germaniae flumine, ubi iis frequenter utuntur
passages.english: *Rhenones* are coverings for the shoulders and chest down to the navel, so shaggy with twisted tufts that they shed the rain; people commonly call them *repti*, because the length of the tufts as it were creeps (*reptat*). Of these Sallust [says]: "The Germans cover their otherwise bare bodies with *rhenones*." They are called *rhenones* from the Rhine, a river of Germany, where they are often worn.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'ltheno' read as 'Rheno'; stray 'q' and page number 454 omitted. 'Quos vulgo reptos vocant' is ungrammatically placed in the Latin; the etymology from *reptare* is Isidore's.

passages.original: 1. Pallium est quo ministrantium scapulæ conteguntur, ut dum ministrant expediti discurrant. Plautus: Si quid facturus es, appende in humeris pallium, Et pergat, quantum valet, tuorum pedum pernicitas. Dictum autem pallium a pellibus, quia prius super indumenta pellicia veteres utebantur, quasi pellea, nive a pala per derivationem.
passages.english: The *pallium* is what covers the shoulders of servants, so that while they serve they may run about unhindered. Plautus: "If you are going to do something, hang your *pallium* on your shoulders, and let the swiftness of your feet go as fast as it can." The *pallium* is named from skins (*pelles*), because the ancients used to wear [it] made of skin over their clothes, as if *pellea*; or else from *pala* by derivation.
passages.notes: 'nive' read as 'sive' (or else).

passages.original: 11. n Diplois, Graecum nomen, ab eo quod sit duplex amictus. Horatius : Contra quem duplici panno patientia velat.
passages.english: *Diplois* is a Greek name, from the fact that it is a double cloak. Horace: "Against whom patience veils herself in a doubled cloth."
passages.notes: Stray 'n' omitted.

passages.original: 2. Nimbus est fasciola transversa ex auro assuta in linleo, quod est in fronte feminarum. Plautus : Quo magis eam aspicio, tam magis nimbata est. a Nam et lumen qUod circa angelorum capita pingitur nitnbus vocatur, licet et nimbus sit densitas nubis.
passages.english: The *nimbus* is a transverse band of gold sewn onto linen, which is worn on women's foreheads. Plautus: "The more I look at her, the more *nimbata* she is." For the light painted around the heads of angels is also called a *nimbus*, although *nimbus* is also a thickness of cloud.
passages.notes: 'linleo' read as 'linteo', 'nitnbus' as 'nimbus'; stray 'a' omitted. *Nimbata* is literally 'banded with a nimbus', perhaps meaning 'showily adorned'.

passages.original: o Monile ornamentum ex gemmis est, quod solet ex feminarum pendere collo, dictum a munere. P Hoc etiam et serpentum dicitur, quia constat ex amphorulis quibusdam aureis, gemmisque variis in modum facturae serpentis. q Nonnulli hoc et segmentum dicunt, ut Juvenalis : Segmenta, et longos habitus ; licet et segmentatas vestes dicamus ut ipse : Et segmentatis dormisset parvuia cunis.
passages.english: A *monile* is an ornament of gems that usually hangs from women's necks, named from *munus* (gift). This is also called a 'serpent' (*serpentum*), because it consists of certain little golden jars and various gems made in the fashion of a serpent. Some also call this a *segmentum*, as Juvenal: "Ornaments (*segmenta*) and long robes"; although we also speak of *segmentatae* garments, as he himself [says]: "And he would have slept in a little cradle trimmed with ornaments (*segmentatis*)."
passages.notes: Stray letters o, P, q omitted; 'parvuia' read as 'parvula'.

passages.original: 8. Fasciola est quae ambit extremitatem vestium, aut ex filis, aut ex auro contexta, assutaque extrinsecus in extrema parte vestimenti, vel chlamydis. De qua Virgilius : Sidoniam piclo chlamydem circumdata limbo.
passages.english: The *fasciola* is what runs round the edge of garments, woven either of threads or of gold, and sewn on the outside at the edge of a garment or of a *chlamys* (cloak). Of which Virgil [says]: "Wrapped in a Sidonian *chlamys* with an embroidered border."
passages.notes: 'piclo' read as 'picto'. The term defined here is evidently the *limbus* (border), as the Virgil quotation suggests; the heading may be corrupt.

passages.original: 10. d Jantaculum est primus cibus quo jejunium solvitur, unde et nuncupatum. Nigidius : Nos ipsi jejunia jantaculi, levibus polluimus.
passages.english: Jantaculum (breakfast) is the first food by which a fast is broken, and it is named from that. Nigidius: "We ourselves have polluted our fasts with light breakfasts."
passages.notes: The quotation appears corrupt; the order 'jejunia jantaculi, levibus' is uncertain and the rendering approximate.

passages.original: 13. h Annona, tractum est a tempore quo Romani veteres ad cibos adrocabantur, sic Martialis : Imperat excelsos frangere nona toros, quod et usque hodie Persæ faciunt.
passages.english: *Annona* is drawn from the time (the ninth hour, *nona*) at which the ancient Romans were summoned to their meals; thus Martial: "The ninth [hour] bids [us] press the high couches"; which the Persians still do even today.
passages.notes: 'adrocabantur' read as 'advocabantur'; stray 'h' omitted. The passage seems abridged or corrupt: the link between *annona* and *nona* is implied but not stated.

passages.original: 36. Mel Graecae appellationis est, quod ab apibus nomen habere probatur. Nam apis Graece μέλισσα dicitur. a Antea autem mella de rore erant, inveniebanturque in arundinum foliis, unde Virgilius : Protinus aerii mellis cælestia dona. i Siquidem hucusque 491 in India et Arabia colliga. tum reperitur, ramis inhaerens in similitudinem salis. Omne autem mel dulce dicitur. c Sardum, amarum est absinthii causa, cujus copia ejus regionis apes nutriuntur.
passages.english: *Mel* (honey) is a Greek name, which is shown to take its name from bees, for a bee in Greek is called *melissa*. Formerly, honey came from dew and was found on the leaves of reeds; hence Virgil: "Next [I shall sing] the heavenly gifts of airborne honey." Indeed, up to now it is found collected in India and Arabia, clinging to branches like salt. All honey is called sweet. Sardinian [honey] is bitter because of wormwood, on the abundance of which the bees of that region feed.
passages.notes: Stray letters and page number 491 omitted; 'colliga. tum' read as 'collectum'. The sentence 'all honey is called sweet' perhaps originally read 'all honey is sweet, [but]'.

passages.original: 3. Crateray calix est duas habens ansas, et est Graecum nomen; declinatur autem apud eos, hic crater. m Nam Latine hac cratera dicitur. Unde Persius : Si tibi crateras argenti... Virgilius : Crateras magnos statuunt, e! vina coronant.
passages.english: A *crater* is a cup having two handles, and it is a Greek name; among them it is declined [masculine] *hic crater*. For in Latin it is called *haec cratera*. Hence Persius: "If [you have] bowls of silver..." Virgil: "They set up great bowls and crown the wine."
passages.notes: 'Crateray' read as 'Crater'; 'hac' as 'haec'; stray 'm' omitted.

passages.original: 1. Omnia vasa coquendi causa parata o cocula dicuntur. Plautus: Æneis oculis mihi excocta est omnis misericordia.
passages.english: All vessels prepared for cooking are called *cocula*. Plautus: "With bronze eyes all pity has been cooked out of me."
passages.notes: Stray 'o' omitted. The Plautus line probably originally read 'aeneis coculis' (in bronze pots); 'oculis' (eyes) looks like an error, but rendered as printed.

passages.original: Focus, quia ϕω̃ς Graece, Latine ignis est, unde juxta philosophos quosdam cuncta procreantur. Et revera sine calore nihil nascitur, adeo, ut de Septentrione poeta dicat n sterili non quidquam frigore gigni. 506 Varro° autem focos ait dictos, quod foveant ignes, nam ignis ipsa flamma est; quidquid autem ignem fovet, focus vocatur, seu ara sit, sive quid aliud, in quo ignis fovetur.
passages.english: The hearth (focus) [is so called] because φῶς in Greek is "fire" in Latin, from which, according to certain philosophers, all things are brought forth. And indeed without heat nothing is born, so much so that the poet says of the North that nothing is produced in the barren cold. Varro, however, says that hearths (foci) are so called because they keep fires warm (foveant), for fire is the flame itself; but whatever keeps fire warm is called a focus, whether it be an altar or anything else in which fire is kept.
passages.notes: Φῶς actually means "light" in Greek; Isidore equates it with Latin ignis. The stray letters "n" and "°" and the number "506" appear to be footnote marks or page numbers and have been omitted. The poet's line is paraphrased by Isidore and the poet is not named.

passages.original: 2. p Lucerna a lychno dicta est, unde et brevis est lu, ut Juvenalis : Dispositae pinguem nebulam vomuere lucernæ.
passages.english: 2. The lamp (lucerna) is named from lychnus [lamp-wick, Greek lychnos], and therefore the syllable lu is short, as in Juvenal: "The lamps set out spewed forth a greasy fog."
passages.notes: Stray letter 'p' before Lucerna treated as a footnote mark and omitted.

passages.original: t Pheretrum dicitur , quod in eo mortui dere- fantur, et est Graecum nomen. Nam ϕέρετρον dicitur, ὰπὄ τού ϕέρειν id est, a ferendo; nam Latine ta- pulus dicitur, quod super capita hominum feratur, sic Plautus: Capularis senex, id est, vicinus capulo.
passages.english: The bier (pheretrum) is so called because the dead are carried on it, and it is a Greek word. For it is called pheretron, from pherein, that is, from carrying. In Latin it is called capulus, because it is carried above people's heads; thus Plautus: "A coffin-ready old man," that is, one near the coffin.
passages.notes: Stray 't' omitted. Read 'deferantur' for 'dere- fantur' and 'capulus' for 'ta- pulus' (scanning errors). The derivation of capulus from caput (head) is implied.

passages.original: 9. Sedes dictae, quod apud veteres Romanos non erat usus accubendi, unde et considere dicebantur. Postea, ut Varro ait de Vita populi Romnni: c Viri discumbere cæperunt, mulieres sedere, quia turpis visus est in muliere accubitus. Sedes singulari numero proprie regni est, qui Græce θρόνος dicitur.
passages.english: 9. Seats (sedes) are so called because among the ancient Romans there was no custom of reclining [at meals], whence they were also said to "sit together" (considere). Later, as Varro says in On the Life of the Roman People, "The men began to recline at table, the women to sit, because reclining seemed indecent in a woman." Sedes in the singular properly belongs to royal power; in Greek it is called θρόνος (throne).
passages.notes: "Romnni" read as "Romani"; the stray "c" before the quotation is taken as a footnote mark and omitted.

passages.original: 4. k Pilentum, vel petoritum, contexta quatuor rotarum vehicula , quibus matronæ olim utebantur. Virgilius: Pilentis matres in mollibus. Horatius: Plures calones atque caballi Pascndi, ducenda petorrita. Erant autem antea pilenta venet coloris , non ut nunc sunt russati, quibus nisi castæ matronæ uti non poterant, sicut nec vittis.
passages.english: 4. The pilentum, or petoritum: four-wheeled wickerwork vehicles which matrons once used. Virgil: "Mothers in soft carriages." Horace: "More grooms and horses must be fed, carriages must be drawn." Formerly, moreover, carriages were sea-blue in colour, not red as they are now, and only chaste matrons could use them, just as [only they could use] fillets.
passages.notes: Stray 'k' omitted. Read 'Pascendi' for 'Pascndi' and 'veneti' for 'venet'. The Virgil quotation is truncated here ("pilentis matres in mollibus").

passages.original: i. c Vomer dictus, quod vi humum eruat, seu ab evomendo terram. De quo Lucretius : Uncus aratri Ferreus, occulto decrescit vomer in arvis. d Sumitque per detrimenta fulgorem.
passages.english: The ploughshare (vomer) is so called because it digs up the ground by force (vi), or from 'vomiting forth' (evomere) the earth. Lucretius says of it: "The iron hook of the plough, the ploughshare, wears away unseen in the fields." And through this wearing away it takes on a shine.
passages.notes: Stray 'c' and 'd' omitted; the leading 'i.' is probably a section number misread.

passages.original: 9. ° Cylindrus, lapis est teres in modum columnae, qui a volubilitate nomen accep t, de quo Virgilius : Area cum primis ingenti æquanda cylindro, Et vertenda manu.
passages.english: 9. The cylinder (cylindrus) is a stone, rounded like a column, which took its name from its rolling. Virgil says of it: "Above all, the threshing floor must be levelled with a huge roller, and turned by hand."
passages.notes: Stray '°' omitted; read 'accepit' for 'accep t'.

passages.original: i. Rota y dicta, quod quasi ruat. Est enim machina de qua a flumine aqua extrahitur. Lucretius : Ut fluvios versare rotas, atque haustra videmus.
passages.english: The wheel (rota) is so called because it is as it were rushing (ruat). For it is a machine by which water is drawn out of a river. Lucretius: "As we see rivers turn wheels and buckets."
passages.notes: Stray 'y' omitted; leading 'i.' probably a misread section number.
